visits.text: Five cone-shaped domes rise like bubbles from the ground in Lasipalatsi Square. They are the skylights of Amos Rex, an art museum that opened in 2018, with galleries built beneath the square. The museum’s address is Lasipalatsi, or “Glass Palace,” a Functionalist building from 1936 with simple lines and no ornamentation. Tickets cost €20 online, and admission is free for visitors under 18. On weekends, the museum is open from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. It is closed on Tuesdays and during exhibition changeovers.

visits.text: Climb to the top of Aulanko Observation Tower, a 33 m granite tower built in 1906–1907 on Aulangonvuori Hill. From the top, the view stretches across the Lake Vanajavesi valley. An old stone staircase then leads down to Bear Cave, where a family of bears sculpted by Robert Stigell rests at the foot of the rock. The tower is free to enter and opens daily from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., from Mother’s Day in May through the end of October.

activities.text: Everything at Aulanko looks wild, yet this forest park was designed. In 1883, Colonel Hugo Standertskjöld bought the estate and turned it into an English landscape park, that is, a garden that imitates nature, with artificial ponds, scenic overlooks, and trees from elsewhere. Walk around Swan Lake (Joutsenlampi), then look for the Ruusulaakso pavilion, decorated with carved wood, and the granite castle ruins, now a summer theater for children. The site has been a nature reserve since 1930: stay on the paths.

In 2018, Hämeenlinna named a wooded area on the eastern shore of Lake Aulanko Sibelius Forest. A nature trail follows the water, with signs explaining the trees and landscape. According to the city, Aulanko’s scenery inspired the composer, particularly in Finlandia, a patriotic work from 1899. Allow 45 minutes for the walk. Hämeenlinna train station, a few kilometers away, then offers a way back to Helsinki or Tampere by train.

activities.text: Helsinki residents call the statue in the small Kolmikulma Park “Diana,” although it depicts Tellervo, the forest goddess in Finnish mythology. The Design District was founded around this triangular park in 2005, when designers and local business owners joined forces. Today, the district brings together about 200 members across 25 streets, offering ceramics, jewelry, Finnish fashion, galleries, and secondhand stores. Look for the small black logo in storefront windows: it identifies businesses that belong to the district.

visits.text: Gustaf Nyström, the architect of the Old Market Hall, also designed the Design Museum (Designmuseo) building in 1894. Today, this museum and the former Museum of Architecture together form the Museum of Architecture and Design (Arkkitehtuuri- ja designmuseo). Its collections trace Finnish design and architecture, from early classics to recent creations. It is open from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., except on Mondays from September through May. Admission is free for visitors under 18.

visits.text: Gravel lanes and colorful wooden houses: Ekenäs Old Town (Gamla stan) has retained its street layout since the 16th century. King Gustav Vasa granted Ekenäs town status in 1546. Four years later, some of its merchants and craftspeople had to leave, willingly or by force, to populate a new town: Helsinki. Look for the “gossip mirrors” mounted outside windows to watch the street without being seen. The market takes place on Wednesdays and Saturdays.

The bell tower overlooking the old town belongs to Ekenäs Church (Ekenäs kyrka), a granite church completed around 1680. A fire devastated it in June 1821: only the altarpiece and a few objects were saved. Architect Charles Bassi rebuilt it between 1839 and 1842, with a roof about 10 m lower and larger windows. Inside, look at the altarpiece, the large painted panel behind the altar, made in Stockholm around 1660.

To understand Ekenäs, nothing beats 1 hour at the Raseborg Museum (Raseborgs museum). Despite its name, it is in the heart of Ekenäs: Raseborg is the municipality that has included the town since 2009. A permanent exhibition is devoted to Helene Schjerfbeck (1862–1946), one of Finland’s best-known painters. She lived in Ekenäs from 1925 to 1941 and painted many of the town’s residents. The museum is closed on Mondays and stays open until 8 p.m. on Wednesdays.

Small in size, big in architectural pedigree: Villa Skeppet (“the ship” in Swedish) is the last and smallest private house designed by Alvar Aalto, a major figure in Finnish architecture. He designed it as a gift of friendship for writer Göran Schildt and his wife Christine. In the living room, the fireplace takes the form of an abstract sculpture. Visits are by guided tour only, in English, in groups of no more than 10 people: book online (€22, about 45 minutes).

activities.text: A 15-minute walk takes you to Ramsholmen Nature Reserve, about 1 km from the center of Ekenäs. Across 55 hectares, small footbridges connect several islets covered in deciduous forest, where some trees exceed 35 m in height. In spring, wood anemones carpet the ground with flowers. A beach offers swimming in summer. The reserve is protected: dogs must stay on a leash, and fires and camping are prohibited.

activities.text: Esplanadi is a narrow park lined with linden trees, between Market Square and Erottaja Square. At the harbor end, the Havis Amanda fountain by sculptor Ville Vallgren dates from 1908. In the middle of the park, the statue of national poet Johan Ludvig Runeberg is the work of his own son, Walter. The Kappeli restaurant, built in 1867, occupies the end of the park nearest the market. Opposite it, Espa Stage, the park’s bandstand, hosts free concerts from May through late August.

visits.text: The village of Fiskars grew up around an ironworks in 1649. That year, Queen Christina of Sweden, who also ruled Finland at the time, authorized businessman Peter Thorwöste to produce iron here. This royal authorization had just one restriction: no cannons. Walk up the village street, lined with former ironworks buildings now used as workshops, including the copper smithy and the granary. At the top of the street, the Clock Tower Building has a Finnish clock that has kept time for the village since 1842.

Warm bread to sample in summer in the old bakery, gardening tools from bygone days on display: the Fiskars Museum (Fiskarsin museo) tells the story of ironworks workers’ lives from the 17th century to the present. Look for the pair of scissors said to be the smallest ever made in Finland. It is a reminder that the Fiskars brand is famous for its orange-handled scissors. The museum opens daily in summer and Wednesday through Sunday during the rest of the year, except in January and February.

activities.text: Set out from the village center for the Rissla Forest Trail (Risslan metsäpolku), a loop of about 4 km marked in orange. It leads to the old Rissla dam, built in 1899 along with a power plant to supply electricity to the factory. Just downstream, the stream drops about 18 m over roughly 100 m, forming a waterfall. The waterfall is fuller in spring and can almost disappear after a dry summer. The trail starts with a steep climb: bring sturdy shoes and mosquito repellent.

If you enjoy handmade objects, set aside 1 hour for the workshops in Fiskars. When the factory left the village in the 1980s, artists and craftspeople took over the empty buildings. Ceramicists, glassmakers, jewelers, and furniture makers work here today, and several open their workshops to visitors. The Fiskars shop also sells the brand’s current products, including its scissors, which are no longer made here. In summer, most shops open daily.

visits.text: A tepee-inspired silhouette and a large window behind the altar define Hailuoto Church. Architects Irma and Matti Aaltonen completed it in 1972. It replaces a church built in 1620 that was destroyed by fire in 1968. In the entrance hall, a small museum displays objects saved from the flames. The church stands in the heart of the island’s main village: visit it first before driving west toward Marjaniemi.

If you’re on the island on a summer weekend, set aside 1 hour for the Kniivilä Museum (Kniivilän kotiseutumuseo). Records of this farm date back to the 1600s. Its last residents were three unmarried siblings, and the interior has been preserved almost exactly as they left it. You’ll see more than 3,000 objects, a shoemaker’s workshop, a cowshed, and a small smoke sauna with no chimney. Since 2024, the exhibition “Meren sylissä” (In the Arms of the Sea) has told the story of the island and its inhabitants. Admission is €5 and free for visitors under 18; card payments only.

The name of the Ojakylä windmill, Hyväntuulen mylly, is a play on words. In Finnish, “tuuli” means both “wind” and “mood”: this is both the mill of fair winds and the mill of good spirits. This traditional windmill is surrounded by old grain storehouses and a large cogwheel. According to local tradition, women turn it every summer to obtain a good grain harvest in the fall. An old sign on the main road points the way, and parking is available.

Your voice echoes back amplified beneath Organum’s three concrete domes in Ulkokarvo. This sound art installation tunes each dome to its own resonant frequency. This is the pitch at which the enclosed air vibrates most readily: a sound close to that pitch is amplified and sustained. Step inside a dome to sing, speak, or play an instrument. Spend a moment in silence, too, listening to the surrounding sounds.

Marjaniemi Lighthouse has watched over Hailuoto’s western tip since 1871. This 25 m brick tower, designed by architect Axel Hampus Dalström, is described as Finland’s best-preserved brick lighthouse. It still guides boats, so visits are guided, last 15 minutes, and take place in groups of about 5 people. A narrow spiral staircase with 110 steps leads to the top. Admission costs €10, with no reservations. In 2026, the lighthouse was open daily from 12 p.m. to 3 p.m., June 19 to August 9.

activities.text: Since June 29, 2026, a ferry has no longer been needed to reach Hailuoto Island. The fixed link, an 8.4 km road made up of two bridges and a causeway, starts at Riutunkari on the mainland. The crossing takes about 8 minutes. The former ferry took 25 to 30 minutes, and in summer, the wait in line could last hours. Hailuoto is the largest island in the Bothnian Bay, the northern part of the Gulf of Bothnia. It has fewer than 1,000 residents. Drive slowly on the island: there are many cyclists.

At Kirkkosalmi, a reed-covered lake occupies what was once an inlet of the sea. The land on Hailuoto is rising by about 1 cm per year. The Earth’s crust, long compressed by the weight of glaciers, has been slowly rebounding since they melted. This is how the lake became cut off from the sea. Its wheelchair-accessible observation tower offers views of cormorants and birds of prey in spring.

Follow the trail’s old yellow markers to the Keskiniemi pooki on Hailuoto’s northern coast. A pooki is a daymark: a landmark built on the coast that sailors can see from a distance to determine their position. Completed in 1858, this one warned ships of the sandbanks north of the headland. It is the island’s oldest surviving daymark. The Finnish Transport Infrastructure Agency restored it in the fall of 2024.

On an almost flat island, Hyypänmäki offers the most beautiful forest walk. This ridge of pine trees and sandy slopes rises to about 31 m, making it Hailuoto’s highest point. Its easy trails start at the Hyypä ski lodge. According to local tradition, the Piilopirtti gorge, “the hidden cabin,” served as a refuge during the Great Northern War (1700–1721). The war pitted Sweden, which Finland was then part of, against Russia. Look for the Hyypä scenic bench, too, a work created by local residents.

If the wind is strong, stroll through the narrow lanes of the fishing village of Marjaniemi. Its small cabins cluster together for shelter from the wind blowing in from the sea. The village is mostly active in summer, but its harbor remains one of Bothnian Bay’s important fishing ports. Around the lighthouse, wooden boardwalks cross dunes and sandy beaches protected as natural areas. Facing west, the headland is a good place to watch the sun set over the sea.

days_plan.itin_title: Oulu in 3 Days: Hailuoto Island and Liminka Bay

visits.text: Red brick, rare in Finland, makes up most of Häme Castle (Hämeen linna). Construction began in the 13th century. It later served as a prison until 1953 and was once the country’s only women’s prison. Explore the Knights’ Hall and the Queen’s Chamber, then the church hall with its medieval wooden statues. Allow 2 hours and budget €15 for admission; the guide on your phone is free. Outside the summer season, the castle is closed on Mondays.

Graffiti left by inmates still covers the cell walls at Vankila, the prison museum next to Häme Castle. Opened in 1871, it was Finland’s first prison to house each inmate in a separate cell. It remained in operation until 1993. Holograms tell the prisoners’ stories, and an exhibition explains their tattoos. The cells are narrow, and the doorways have raised thresholds. The museum opens only during the warmer months: in 2026, through September 30.

Step inside Jean Sibelius’s birthplace (Sibeliuksen syntymäkoti) at 11 Hallituskatu. The composer was born here on December 8, 1865, and spent his first twenty years in Hämeenlinna. The rooms, furnished in the style of the 1860s through the 1880s, contain family letters, drawings, and a travel piano. Chamber music concerts take place in the house’s hall. The museum opens Tuesday through Sunday, from noon to 4 p.m. in winter and from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. in summer.

To see how a well-to-do Hämeenlinna family lived a century ago, stop by Palander House. Built in 1861, the home has been restored to its appearance from the 1890s through the 1920s. The tour takes you from the formal drawing room to the servants’ kitchen, revealing the lives of both the owners and their staff. Allow 45 minutes for the visit. Check the hours carefully: from September through May, the house opens only on Saturdays and Sundays, from noon to 4 p.m.

Hämeenlinna Church (Hämeenlinnan kirkko), on the market square, is round like the Pantheon in Rome, which served as its model. It was built between 1792 and 1798 to designs by Louis Jean Desprez, a French architect at the Swedish court. Then head to Sibelius Park downtown, where a bronze statue of the composer by Kain Tapper has stood since 1964. Sit on one of the four benches with motion sensors: they play excerpts from his series of pieces devoted to trees.

days_plan.itin_title: Tampere and Häme in 4 Days: Castle, Glass, and Art

visits.text: Hanko’s most beautiful side is built of wood: the villas on its southern tip. After the spa resort opened in 1879, wealthy families, some from St. Petersburg, had villas built here with intricately crafted wooden facades. They are nicknamed “lace villas.” Most still stand around the spa park (Kylpyläpuisto) and along Bulevardi. Beside Plagen Beach, the Casino, an events hall dating from 1879, offers no gambling: it is a summer restaurant.

Between 1880 and 1930, about 250,000 Finns left their country through the port of Hanko, bound for the United States, Canada, or Australia. Hanko Museum (Hangon museo) tells their stories in its exhibition “Where the Land Meets the Sea,” which opened in 2025. It also explores life in the villas, industry, and the peninsula’s natural environment. The museum occupies a former mechanical engineering factory, with no steps or thresholds. It is open Tuesday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and on weekends from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m.

Hanko Front Museum (Hangon rintamamuseo) is in Lappohja, on the road to Ekenäs, about 21 km from Hanko, a 20-minute drive. In March 1940, the peace agreement that ended the Winter War against the Soviet Union required Finland to lease the Hanko Peninsula to the Soviets for 30 years as a naval base. The base’s boundary ran about a hundred meters from the museum. The Soviets left as early as December 1941. Behind the building, a trail of about 1 km follows the trenches. Open Tuesday through Sunday from June to August, and just one day a week during the rest of the year.

activities.text: Walk to the very end of mainland Finland along the 6.7 km Tulliniemi nature trail. It crosses pine forest, dry meadows, and rounded rocks to reach Uddskatan, the point where the Gulf of Finland meets the Archipelago Sea. About half a million migrating birds pass over this point each year. Since 1979, a bird observatory has counted them and fitted numbered bands to their legs to track their journeys. The trail is for pedestrians only.

A guest book carved into rock: that is the nickname of Hauensuoli, the “pike’s gut,” a narrow channel between two islets off Tulliniemi. Sailors waiting here for favorable winds carved their names and coats of arms into the rock—the designs that served as emblems for noble families. There are more than 600 carvings, the oldest dating from the 15th century. The boat leaves from East Harbor (Itäsatama), and the trip lasts about 2 hours.

Climb to the Emigrant Monument on the rocks along Merikatu, facing the sea: three cranes take flight toward the open water. An association erected it together with 93 Finnish municipalities, each of which had lost more than a tenth of its population to emigration. Continue onto Puistovuori along the “Path of Love” (Rakkauden polku), about 1.5 km long, laid out in the late 19th century for spa resort guests. Emigrants are said to have come to dance on its flat rock while waiting for their ships.

visits.text: Suomenlinna Fortress spreads across six interconnected islands at the entrance to Helsinki's harbour—the ferry crossing from Market Square takes just 20 minutes. Built by Sweden starting in 1748 under Admiral Augustin Ehrensvärd to counter Russian expansion, it became one of the Swedish Empire's largest 18th-century projects, mobilising over 6,500 Finnish and Swedish soldiers. Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991, the fortress is still home to 850 permanent residents today. Set aside half a day: the ramparts, tunnels, King's Gate (the original sea entrance), museums, and sea views are all worth exploring. In summer, Helsinki locals picnic on the bastions in the evening—a quintessentially Finnish scene.

Helsinki Cathedral has crowned Senate Square since 1852—its green dome is visible from the harbour. Carl Ludvig Engel worked on this project from 1818 until his death in 1840; the building was completed twelve years later. Originally built as St. Nicholas Church in honour of Tsar Nicholas I, it was renamed after Finland's independence in 1917. Senate Square itself is an exceptional neoclassical ensemble: Engel designed all four buildings surrounding it—the cathedral, government palace, university, and national library. A musical carillon plays from the square every day at 5:49 PM.

Temppeliaukio Church is carved directly into bedrock—architects Timo and Tuomo Suomalainen won the competition in 1961, after several previous designs from the 1930s had been abandoned. Construction began in February 1968 and the church was consecrated in September 1969. The 24-metre copper dome rests on concrete beams that allow natural light to filter between the raw rock and the cupola. The acoustics are so exceptional that the space regularly serves as a concert hall. Nearly 500,000 people visit each year.

Uspenski Orthodox Cathedral overlooks the harbour from its red-brick hill, with its golden domes - designed by Russian architect Aleksey Gornostayev and completed in 1868. From the forecourt, the view extends across the harbour, with Suomenlinna island in the background.

The Kallio district, north of the centre, is a lively, alternative counterpart to tourist Helsinki. Kallio Church, designed by Lars Sonck and completed in 1912 in the National Romantic style, dominates the district from its hill - its bells play a Sibelius chorale. Hakaniemi Market Hall (1914) sells smoked fish and artisan cheeses in a renovated red-brick hall.

The Ateneum is Finland's national gallery—the country's most important art collection, from 19th-century Finnish masters like Albert Edelfelt and Helene Schjerfbeck through to 20th-century expressionists. The 1887 Neo-Renaissance building faces Central Railway Station. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours.

Kiasma, the contemporary art museum designed by American architect Steven Holl and opened in 1998, is an architectural sculpture in the heart of the city - its curved façade plays with natural light throughout the day.

The Finlayson Quarter was born in 1820 when Scotsman James Finlayson opened a textile workshop on the Tammerkoski rapids—this is where Tampere's industrial story truly begins, earning the city its nickname as the 'Manchester of Finland'. The red brick buildings have been converted into a lively district of shops, cinemas, restaurants, and museums. In the old machine building, the Finnish Labour Museum Werstas preserves in its original location the massive Sulzer engine purchased in 1900 to power the factory. Admission to Werstas is free.

The Moomin Museum, housed in Tampere Hall since 2017, is the world's only museum entirely dedicated to Tove Jansson's universe. It holds the original ink and watercolour illustrations as well as the three-dimensional Moominvalley dioramas built by Jansson herself and her partner Tuulikki Pietilä. Jansson donated her collection to the Tampere Art Museum in 1986. These aren't reproductions—they're the original drawings in their original state. Allow 1.5 to 2 hours.

Pyynikki Observation Tower stands on the Pyynikki gravel ridge, a remnant of the last Ice Age. The current tower dates from 1929 and was rebuilt after its predecessor was damaged during the Finnish Civil War of 1918. From the top, 26 metres up, the two lakes framing Tampere - Näsijärvi to the north and Pyhäjärvi to the south - can be seen at the same time. The tower café serves famous munkki (fried doughnuts) - do not leave without trying one.

Nuuksio National Park, 30 km west of Helsinki, is the region's green lung - glacial lakes, conifer forests and flying squirrels. If you have half a day before your return flight, it is the most accessible nature escape from the capital. By public transport, take the train to Espoo, then the HSL bus to the park entrance.

Kamppi Chapel of Silence, inaugurated in 2012, is a curved wooden block set in the middle of a busy commercial square—a secular sanctuary open to all, without religious services. The blonde spruce interior and curved walls create unique acoustics and light. Architect Kimmo Lintula won the Finnish Architecture Prize for this project.

The Sibelius Monument, in Sibelius Park northwest of the centre, was sculpted by Eila Hiltunen and unveiled in 1967. It consists of 600 hollow steel pipes welded into a wave-like form—the sculptor wanted to capture the essence of Sibelius's music rather than his portrait. The composer's portrait was eventually added alongside, after public criticism.

activities.text: Kauppatori Market Square is Helsinki's maritime heart—fresh seafood, smoked salmon, wild berries, and local crafts in colourful waterfront stalls. In summer, it's also the departure point for ferries to Suomenlinna and archipelago cruises. Arrive in the morning for the best produce.

The Design District encompasses 25 streets and over 200 shops, galleries, and workshops in the neighbourhood south of the centre. The Design Museum traces how a newly independent nation built a visual identity that eventually produced Marimekko, Iittala, and Fiskars. It's a place to wander—allow 2 hours depending on your interest in design.

The Esplanadi is Helsinki's tree-lined pedestrian boulevard, bordered by terraces between Market Square and the Design District. In the evening, it's where locals gather for drinks on the terrace or free summer concerts. The Akateeminen bookstore at number 39, designed by Alvar Aalto, is also worth a look.

The Löyly public sauna, on the former Hernesaari docks, combines contemporary architecture (wood, glass and sea views) with Finnish tradition. The sauna experience continues with a dip in the sea directly from the terrace. Booking is recommended at weekends.

The Tammerkoski rapids flow through Tampere's centre for 700 metres—it's the water that built the city, powering factories for 150 years. A walk along the banks from Finlayson to the central bridge offers the best overview of the converted industrial city.

The Helsinki-Tampere train (1 hour 45 minutes, frequent departures) is the most convenient way to make this day trip. Leave early morning from Helsinki Central Station, spend the day in Tampere, and return to Helsinki in the evening to sleep before the next day's flight to Rovaniemi. No need to rent a car for this leg.

Tampere Market Hall (Kauppahalli, 1901) is the place to try mustamakkara - Tampere's black sausage, made with blood and oats and served with lingonberry jam. It is an emblematic speciality of the city. The market also has bakeries, fishmongers and cafés.

The South Harbour is a pleasant place for a final walk in Helsinki. Follow the quays from Market Square to enjoy views of the sea and Suomenlinna island in the background. In summer, the low evening light accompanies the walk, even after the market stalls have closed.

visits.text: The Sámi, the Indigenous people of northern Scandinavia and Finland, called themselves “vuovjjuš” here, meaning nomads. The Hetta visitor center (Tunturi-Lapin luontokeskus) adopted this word for its free exhibition, which tells the story of how they adapted to the Arctic climate. Another room shows how local people divide the year into eight seasons. In 2025, the center’s summer hours were Monday through Friday, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m.: visit on a weekday.

Simple and austere, Enontekiö Church in Hetta nevertheless holds an enormous artwork behind its altar. The back wall is almost entirely covered by a composition by Uuno Eskola: the risen Christ blesses Lapland and its people. The tundra landscape, a cold, treeless plain, is painted on plaster, while the figures are rendered in mosaic. Look for a figure in Sámi dress and a herd of reindeer. Completed in 1952, the church was funded in part by a donation from Lutheran churches in America. In summer, it is open on weekdays from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., with a guide.

activities.text: Follow the red trail markers from the visitor center to the summit of Jyppyrä, the hill overlooking Hetta. The trail is 1.6 km long and leads to an elevation of approximately 400 m. From the top, the view stretches across Lake Ounasjärvi to the chain of Pallas and Ounastunturi peaks. On the opposite shore begins the roughly fifty-kilometer Hetta-Pallas trail, which hikers reach by boat. Head up in the evening: in midsummer, the sun barely sets.

Peurapolku, a 2 km history trail, also starts at the Hetta visitor center. It passes old hunting pits, holes dug in the ground to trap game. One has been reconstructed with its fence, helping explain the technique. The other remains are protected: stay on the trail, marked by posts bearing hoofprints. A covered shelter with a fire pit offers a place to take a break along the way.

visits.text: Orange-red molten glass turns at the ends of blowpipes, the glassblowers’ long tubes. From the visitor gallery at the Iittala glassworks (Iittalan lasitehdas), you can watch them work directly below. The glassworks has been operating since 1881. The Aalto vase, designed in 1936 by architect Alvar Aalto, and designer Oiva Toikka’s glass birds are still mouth-blown here. Admission is free Monday through Friday, from 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. Come on a weekday morning: the gallery is closed on weekends. In summer, it may also close for several weeks: in 2026, it remained closed from June 29 through August 31. Check before visiting between June and August.

Continue your day of art at Visavuori, the home and studio of sculptor Emil Wikström (1864–1942), in Sääksmäki, on the southern shore of Lake Vanajavesi. Allow less than half an hour to drive there from Iittala. Wikström designed the buildings himself and built them between 1893 and 1912: a log house dating from 1902, which retains its original furnishings, and a castle-shaped studio with an observatory and winter garden, where nearly a hundred of his works are displayed. The Kari Pavilion showcases editorial cartoons by his grandson, cartoonist Kari Suomalainen. In summer, a café occupies the former bronze foundry beneath the studio. Along with the Iittala naive art exhibition, Visavuori is part of the “Vanajavesi art triangle.” Check opening hours before visiting.

The Iittala naive art exhibition (Naivistit Iittalassa) displays paintings by around fifty artists each summer. Naive art is a direct, highly colorful style of painting that often tells the story of the artist’s life. The exhibition began in 1989 in the village’s old wooden schoolhouse. Today, it is held at the Glass Centre, the glass center in the heart of Iittala. It opens daily from mid-May through late August, then on weekends from November through March for a winter exhibition devoted to the history of naive art.

In 1921, the municipality of Kalvola completed its church, built from its own granite. Kalvola Church stands near Iittala. This village was the administrative center of Kalvola, a municipality incorporated into Hämeenlinna in 2009. Stop for 15 minutes along the way to see the stone up close. A parish member sometimes shows visitors around the church.

activities.text: You will finish your stop at Lasimäki, Iittala’s “glass hill,” where the shops are clustered. Iittala Outlet sells glassware and tableware from Iittala, Arabia, Fiskars, and Hackman. The small shops nearby offer crafts, home decor, and gourmet foods. Bistro Alvar serves lunch on-site. Wrap your glass purchases in your clothes before getting back on the road.

visits.text: Siida, in Inari, brings together Finland’s Sámi Museum and a nature information center for the Far North. In Sámi, a siida is a group of herding families whose reindeer graze together. The main exhibition, redesigned in 2022, explains the connections between Sámi culture and nature. In 2024, Siida received the European Museum of the Year Award. Outside, the open-air museum brings together around fifty historic buildings. Admission: €18. From June through September, Siida opens daily from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.; from October through May, it is closed on Sundays.

A parliament on the banks of a river in Lapland: this is Sajos, Inari’s Sámi cultural center. The building houses the Sámi Parliament, the assembly representing Finland’s Sámi people. It also houses their archives and a training center. Sajos opened in 2012. Its facades face the Juutua, where the river flows into Lake Inari. Admission is free. On weekdays, a guided tour introduces the Parliament and contemporary Sámi life. Café Čaiju serves lunch from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.

activities.text: Follow the Juutua, the river flowing through Inari, on a 6.3 km loop starting from the village. The trail follows the south bank upstream to the Jäniskoski rapids. It crosses them on a footbridge, then returns along the north bank. Along the way, laavu, wooden shelters open on one side, offer places to take a break around a fire. Allow 2 hours of walking. The trail is lit and maintained in winter, making it a good outing in December, when the sun no longer rises.

Four and a half kilometers of forest separate the parking lot from Pielpajärvi Church, and that is what gives it its charm. It was built between 1752 and 1760. In the 17th century, Inari’s Sámi families moved with the seasons to fish and hunt. In winter, they gathered here in a village that also hosted markets and court sessions. The trail starts at a parking lot on Sarviniementie Road, 2.5 km from the main road. The round trip is 9 km. The church remains accessible year-round.

You will board at the harbor next to Siida for a cruise of 2 hours 30 minutes on Lake Inari. It is Finland’s third-largest lake, with 3,318 islands. The boat circles Ukonsaari, a rocky island about 30 m high that is sacred to the Sámi. There is no landing on the island: tradition holds that a sacred place should not be entered without a reason. The lake is frozen from November to early June, so cruises only run in summer.

visits.text: In central Ivalo, St. Nicholas Orthodox Church tells the story of the Skolt Sámi. This Sámi group, whose faith is Orthodox Christianity, lived in Petsamo. After World War II, the territory became part of the Soviet Union, and the Skolts were resettled in the municipality of Inari. Originally a simple chapel in 1960, the building became a church in 1994. Stop for 15 minutes before heading to the airport.

activities.text: No airport in the European Union lies farther north than Ivalo Airport. The terminal is in Törmänen, 11 km from the village of Ivalo and 25 km from Saariselkä, your first stop. Car rental companies have counters here. A shuttle to Saariselkä leaves from outside the terminal. The shuttle to Inari operates by reservation only.

You will head to Ivalo Airport, 11 km southwest of the village, to return the car. Ivalo sits on the Ivalojoki River. In 1870, about 500 prospectors flocked here during Lapland’s first gold rush. Finnair connects Ivalo with Helsinki year-round, and other airlines add seasonal direct flights to Europe.

visits.text: Skata, also known as Norrmalm, is Jakobstad’s old neighborhood of colorful wooden houses. According to the city, it is one of Finland’s largest continuous areas of historic wooden houses. Until the late 18th century, it was inhabited mainly by sailors and their families. It later became the neighborhood of workers at the Strengberg tobacco factory, the city’s largest employer around 1900. Protected since 1982, it can be explored on foot; the tourist office organizes guided tours by reservation.

Shipowner and merchant Peter Malm had Malm House (Malmska gården) built; it now houses the Jakobstad Museum. Founded in 1904, the museum focuses mainly on seafaring and shipbuilding. The name Jakobstad means “Jacob’s town.” Ebba Brahe founded it in 1652 and named it after her late husband, Jacob De la Gardie. Open Tuesday through Saturday from noon to 4 p.m.; admission €7, or €12 including the Tempus exhibition hall.

A 65 m spire marks Pedersöre Church, one kilometer south of downtown Jakobstad. Its oldest sections, built of stone, date from the 15th century. Starting in 1787, it was expanded into the shape of a cross with four equal arms. In July 1985, a fire destroyed the spire, altarpiece, and organ; the church was restored as early as 1986. The interior can only be visited by appointment; otherwise, walk around the building.

If you are traveling with children, stop at Skolparken, Jakobstad’s “school park.” This botanical garden was created in the early 20th century for schoolchildren’s botany lessons. It contains about 1,000 plant species around a pond where carp swim. Twenty minutes is enough to walk around it, between the museum and the Skata neighborhood.

Until the mid-19th century, the Old Harbor (Gamla hamn) was Jakobstad’s harbor. Its shipyard, Skeppsgården, houses two large wooden sailing ships. The Jacobstads Wapen is a replica of an 18th-century galeas, a two-masted merchant ship, built using plans from 1755. The three-masted schooner Vega was used to pay war reparations, a debt Finland owed the Soviet Union. In 2026, guided tours run from June 1 through July 31, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., for €15.

Nanoq means “polar bear” in Greenlandic. It is the name of Finland’s first Arctic museum, which opened in June 1991. It was founded by Pentti Kronqvist, a retired firefighter and polar explorer. In the forest near Fäboda, a main building and several small cabins tell the stories of the peoples, natural environments, and expeditions of the polar regions. From June through August, it opens Monday through Saturday from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.; during the rest of the year, mainly on Wednesday and Thursday afternoons.

activities.text: You will end the day at Fäboda, about ten kilometers from downtown Jakobstad. Three large sandy beaches alternate with smooth rocks popular with photographers. Marked trails, ranging from a short loop to 33 km, wind through the forest, and an observation tower overlooks the shore. In the evening, settle onto the rocks to watch the sun set over the sea; there is a café near the beaches.

days_plan.itin_title: Ostrobothnia in 4 Days: Vaasa, Kvarken, and Wooden Towns

visits.text: Joensuu was founded in 1848 by Tsar Nicholas I of Russia—its name means 'river mouth,' which describes its location exactly. The 1914 city hall is the work of Eliel Saarinen, the Finnish architect who would later conquer America with the Chicago Tribune Tower. Walk past it; this is one of the finest buildings in eastern Finland.

The North Karelian Museum Hilma, housed in the Carelicum building facing the market square, traces the region's history from prehistoric times through the Soviet-Finnish wars. The permanent exhibition covers the Winter War, Orthodox culture, Karelian traditions, and—surprisingly—Finland's rock scene, including Nightwish. Audio excerpts, reconstructed saunas, and dioramas bring the experience to life for all ages. Plan for an hour and a half.

Joensuu Art Museum Onni occupies a neo-Renaissance former high school from 1894—beautiful building, surprising collection for a city this size. Beyond Finnish art from the 19th century to the present, you'll find a section of Orthodox icons from Eastern Europe, extremely rare in western Finland. If you only have time for one museum, choose Hilma for Karelian history, Onni for art.

Valamo Monastery in Heinävesi—about 100 km southwest of Joensuu, on the return route—is the heart of Orthodox life in Finland. The monastic community took refuge here from Lake Ladoga in 1940, bringing their icons with them. The main church, gardens, museum, and monastery shop (house wines, honey, cheeses) are worth the visit. The place is open to non-believers and the atmosphere is peaceful—nothing like tourist reconstructions.

activities.text: Taitokortteli is a cluster of old wooden houses in the heart of Joensuu—artisan workshops, a Karelian souvenir shop, and a café. This is the place to buy handmade Karelian pasties (karjalanpiirakka) and traditional embroidery. Stop before heading into the forest: you'll have picnic supplies for the road.

Joensuu Market Square and the banks of the Pielisjoki are lively in summer. In the evening, a walk along the river is enough to take in the slow, pleasant rhythm of this university city of 75,000 inhabitants, which remains perfectly human-sized.

If you have time, detour to Parppeinvaara in Ilomantsi—Finland's easternmost municipality, 70 km from Joensuu. The Runopirtti (runic song house) is the place in Finland where you're most likely to hear runes sung: the oral poetic tradition that inspired the Kalevala, the national epic. Guides in period costume sing on request. This is the most authentic detour of the entire itinerary.

Botania, Joensuu's botanical garden and butterfly house, is a green pause to finish—tropical greenhouses with live butterflies in free flight, outdoor garden open year-round. A quiet hour before catching the train or road back to Helsinki.

activities.text: The boat’s engine echoes between two rock walls about 50 m high. This narrow lake, Julma-Ölkky, is the largest of Finland’s three canyon lakes: it stretches for 3 km and measures just 10 m across at its narrowest point. It occupies a fissure in the Earth’s crust dating back more than 2 billion years, later shaped by glaciers. From the boat, you get a better view of the rock paintings, ancient drawings made on the rock. Expect to pay €18 per adult, with tickets available at the parking lot kiosk.

In Finnish, “julma” means “cruel,” and Julma-Ölkky’s terrain lives up to the name. The Ölökyn ylitys trail, “the canyon crossing,” is a loop of about 5.3 km starting at the lake’s parking lot. It features a succession of steep climbs and steel stairways. It crosses the lake on a 45 m suspension bridge. It also passes near Pirunkirkko, “the devil’s church,” a natural cavity in the rock. Allow about 2 hours of hiking. Wear sturdy footwear: the national parks agency rates this trail as demanding.

visits.text: Jussarö has long led sailors astray: the iron ore beneath the island pulls at compass needles, and several ships have been wrecked around its shores. This iron was mined in the 19th century, then again from the late 1950s until 1967, when falling ore prices shut the mine down. The military then used the empty buildings for urban combat training until 2005. The abandoned facilities, described as Finland’s only ghost town, occupy the eastern side of the island. Only part of the site is open to visitors.

activities.text: If you don’t have your own boat, the Myggen III water taxi takes you to Jussarö, an island in Ekenäs Archipelago National Park. Established in 1989, the park is almost 90% water. On the island, a 4.7 km nature trail passes through an old forest and alongside former ore extraction pits. Climb the observation tower where maritime pilots once watched for ships. These pilots were local sailors responsible for guiding boats between submerged rocks.

Red rocks and an open horizon set the scene at Iron Beach, the “iron beach,” a small beach on Jussarö. On clear days, you can watch large ships passing offshore between Finland and Sweden. Along this coast, the sea temperature is around 16 to 17 °C in July and August, making for an invigorating swim. Bring a picnic; there is a barbecue area on the island.

days_plan.itin_title: Finland’s Southern Coast in 3 Days: Fiskars, Ekenäs, and Hanko

visits.text: The Myllykoski mill stands beside the rapids of the Kitkajoki River, on the Pieni Karhunkierros loop. Its name means “mill rapids” in Finnish. Metsähallitus, the public agency that manages the national parks, describes this landscape as possibly the most photographed in Finland. This is where the loop splits: you can choose to walk it in either direction. Come early in the morning: crowds gather during the day, and there are sometimes waits at the nearby suspension bridges.

A 9 m drop over a length of 25 m: Jyrävä waterfall forces the Kitkajoki River through a narrow rock channel. On the International Scale of River Difficulty, it is rated Class VI, the highest level. Only expert teams attempt it, after careful scouting. In winter, a thick arch of ice covers it and rarely melts before May. View it from the trail, keeping your distance, as the wet rock is slippery.

activities.text: From the Juuma parking lot, take the Pieni Karhunkierros trail, the “Little Bear Loop.” This 12 km loop takes 4 to 6 hours and offers a summary of Oulanka National Park: rapids, gorges, overlooks, and three suspension bridges over the water. The route is demanding because of the elevation changes and long wooden staircases. A steep climb up very tall staircases leads to the Kallioportti overlook. Follow the green trail markers. Start early to avoid waiting at the bridges. Bring a picnic: campfire sites line the route.

If you still have energy, head down the Kitkajoki River in a raft, a large inflatable boat led by a guide. Operators in Juuma and the surrounding area offer a family trip lasting 2 hours to 2 hours 30 minutes, open to ages 5 and up. Expect to pay €45 to €49 per adult depending on the operator, based on summer 2026 rates. Wilder trips, lasting 2 hours to 4 hours 30 minutes, are for adults only and cost €69 to €99. Book ahead, especially in July, one of the busiest months.

visits.text: No city in the world has as many buildings by Alvar Aalto as Jyväskylä. The architect grew up here and opened his first office here in 1923. Start at Aalto2, a museum center connecting two buildings he designed: the Alvar Aalto Museum and the Museum of Central Finland. The “AALTO” exhibition tells the story of his life and work, carried out with his two wives, first Aino and then Elissa. One room presents the thirteen works by Aalto that were jointly added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2026. Admission €18; closed Mondays.

Red brick, mahogany railings, and light streaming through skylights: the University of Jyväskylä’s main building, completed in 1955, is the best-known building on the Aalto campus. Its grand staircase leads into the middle of the fan-shaped assembly hall, bringing academic processions into view of everyone present. The campus is among Aalto’s UNESCO-listed works. The building houses a café open to the public. In summer, Aalto2 offers a guided campus tour in English, bookable online.

With columns and windows inspired by the Italian Renaissance, the Workers’ Hall (Työväentalo) hardly matches the usual image of Aalto’s architecture, yet he did design it. Completed in 1925, it was his first major public building. Upstairs, its theater hall was used until 1982, when the new municipal theater opened, also designed by Aalto. View the facade from Väinönkatu, then head to the theater to compare the two periods of the architect’s work.

If you are in town on a summer evening, listen at 8 p.m.: a song has been broadcast every evening from the top of Vesilinna Tower since 1976. This water tower stands atop Harju, a pine-covered sandy ridge at the edge of downtown. Climb up the Nero Steps, built in 1925 to provide work for the unemployed. The tower houses a natural history museum and a café. Its free observation deck is only open during café hours: Tuesday through Friday from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., and Saturday from noon to 6 p.m.

The Craft Museum of Finland (Suomen käsityön museo) deserves an hour of your time for its traditional costumes alone. This national museum explores Finnish craftsmanship in the “Craftstories” exhibition (stories of crafts) and a room devoted to national costume. A fun detail: on August 5, National Costume Day, admission is free for anyone wearing a piece of national costume. The rest of the year, admission is €10, with free entry for visitors under 18. The museum, on Kauppakatu, is open Tuesday through Sunday from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.

activities.text: End the day at Lutakko Harbor, on Lake Jyväsjärvi, in front of Alvar Aalto’s boat. The 10 m Nemo Propheta in Patria was built in Säynätsalo in 1954–1955. The Aaltos used it to reach their summer house in Muuratsalo, which you visit on day 3. Its Latin name means “No one is a prophet in their own land.” It is on permanent display in a purpose-built shelter beside a restaurant-sauna. In summer, lake cruises also depart from Jyväskylä Harbor.

days_plan.itin_title: Central Finland in 4 Days: Aalto, Petäjävesi, and Kuopio

visits.text: If your phone jumps back an hour on the Karesuvanto bridge, that is normal: across the river, Sweden runs on Central European Time. Built in 1980, this bridge connects the Finnish village to Karesuando, its Swedish twin. There, the wooden church built in 1905 is Sweden’s northernmost church. Its 1961 altarpiece, by Swedish artist Bror Hjorth, depicts Pastor Lars Levi Laestadius, founder of a religious revival movement, at the foot of the cross. He preached here from 1826 to 1849. Allow for a walk of about 1 km from one bank to the other.

Trenches, shelters, and machine gun nests, but no real battle: that is the paradox of Järämä. Starting in August 1944, the German army built the Sturmbock defensive line here to protect access to Arctic Ocean ports. It abandoned the line without a fight in January 1945. The restored site features 1,209 m of trenches and a museum about the Lapland War. It is on the E8, about 20 km from Karesuvanto. In 2026, it was open from June 9 to September 19, Tuesday through Saturday, from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Lapland in 5 Days: Levi, Pallas, and Kilpisjärvi

activities.text: The aroma of salmon soup drifts through the aisles of the Old Market Hall (Vanha kauppahalli), beside Market Square (Kauppatori). Opened in 1889, it is the city’s oldest market hall. It is known for this soup and its fish sandwiches. Outside, stalls selling Finnish products and souvenirs become more numerous from spring through fall. In winter, heated tents still serve coffee. Eat here before catching the ferry, which departs from the edge of the square.

days_plan.itin_title: Helsinki in 2 Days: Suomenlinna, Seurasaari, and Design

visits.text: A gold museum in the middle of the forest: welcome to Tankavaara, 30 km south of Saariselkä and about a twenty-minute drive from Kiilopää. Sámi people, the Indigenous people of Lapland, discovered gold here in 1934. The Gold Museum, which opened in 1973, traces gold prospecting in Lapland and more than 20 countries. One wing sits beneath a roof shaped like a gold pan, the shallow bowl used to wash sand to separate out gold. Hours: daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. from June through September, Monday through Friday in winter.

activities.text: No more trees, just low vegetation and wind: this is the summit of Kiilopää, at 546 m. The Kiirunapolku trail, a 6 km loop, starts at the hiking center at the foot of the hill. It climbs 214 m, partly via stairs. From the summit, you can see the hills of Urho Kekkonen National Park, established in 1983. The park is named after a former Finnish president. Allow 2 to 3 hours and bring a warm layer, even in July.

Finns call the steam that rises when water is poured over hot stones löyly. At the Kuurakaltio smoke sauna in Kiilopää, this steam is known for being very gentle. This sauna has no chimney: smoke fills the room as it heats up, then the room is aired out before anyone enters. Between sauna sessions, a pool built into the Kiilo-oja stream awaits the brave, with water temperatures between 5 and 15 °C in summer. Public sessions take place between 3 p.m. and 7:30 p.m., by reservation.

days_plan.itin_title: Northern Lapland in 5 Days: Inari, Saariselkä, and Lemmenjoki

visits.text: At an elevation of 565 m, Muotkatakka is the highest point on Finland’s public roads. This pass on the E8 lies just before the descent to Kilpisjärvi, above the tree line. A rest area and a Lapland War memorial mark the spot. Stop briefly here: around you, the forest gives way entirely to tundra, the low-growing vegetation of cold regions.

activities.text: Hunters once believed that the spirits of Saana brought them luck. This 1,029 m summit rises 556 m above Lake Kilpisjärvi. The marked trail starts at the Malla parking lot and climbs to the summit, following the same route back for a total of about 8 km. A hut with a fire pit marks the first kilometer. Higher up, granite steps installed in 2019 help hikers through the steepest section. Allow four to six hours and bring a warm jacket: snow can fall even in summer.

You will board the M/S Malla at 10 a.m. from the lakeshore at 14678 Käsivarrentie, on the E8. After a 30-minute crossing, a 3 km trail leads to Treriksröset, the three-country border marker. This beige concrete cone, placed about ten meters from shore in 1926, marks the point where Finland, Sweden, and Norway meet. It is also Sweden’s northernmost point. The boat operates from the melting of the ice, around Midsummer, until the second half of September.

You have to step from stone to stone to cross the rocky bed of Skirhasjohka creek on the Saana nature trail. This loop of about 6 km starts at the Malla parking lot and takes two to three hours. It passes the Saana hut, just beyond about twenty stone steps. Around Kilpisjärvi, mountain birches grow no higher than 600 to 700 m above sea level; above that, the mountainside is bare. Bring boots that cover your ankles, as some streams have no bridges and swell after rain.

activities.text: You land at Kittilä Airport, the gateway to Western Lapland. Pick up your rental car on arrival, as the stops on this itinerary are very far apart. Buses to Pallas run mainly on weekdays. Take Route 79 toward Muonio, then turn onto the road to Pallas at Jerisjärvi. Allow for approximately 68 km to reach the national park.

If your flight leaves in the morning, allow less than 15 minutes to drive from Levi to Kittilä Airport via Route 79. Return your rental car at the airport and leave time to refuel beforehand. The route totals approximately 640 km between Pallas, Hetta, Kilpisjärvi, and Levi.

visits.text: A red rock face towers above the white foam of the Kiutaköngäs rapids, one of the highlights of Oulanka National Park. The color comes from dolomite, a rock similar to limestone. Over 325 m, the Oulankajoki River drops 14 m, including a main drop of about 4 m. Along the bank, a channel dug in the early 20th century was used for log driving, the practice of transporting logs downriver. It now fills almost exclusively during floods. The 1 km trail from the visitor center parking lot is open year-round.

activities.text: The Könkään keino trail extends your visit to the rapids with a loop of nearly 8 km, taking 3 to 4 hours including the stop at Kiutaköngäs. It crosses open pine forest, follows the river, then passes peat bogs and damp forests rich in flowers. Beyond the rapids, the highlight is the Loseikko overlook, above the bends of the Oulankajoki River. The route is mostly flat, with a few short climbs. Stop for a picnic at the Merenoja or Kiutaköngäs picnic areas.

Next, let the Oulankajoki River carry you along by canoe from Mataraniemi, 1.5 km from the visitor center. This stretch is rated easy, with no rapids, and suits beginners and families alike. A rental company in Juuma offers an unguided 8 km trip, including equipment and a transfer, starting at €50 per person in a two-person canoe. Those with more stamina can continue 25 km to Jäkälämutka, taking 5 to 7 hours. At Jäkälämutka, a rope prevents canoes from entering the border zone with Russia.

visits.text: The K.H. Renlund Museum is the best introduction to Kokkola’s history, and admission is free. It is named after Karl Herman Renlund, who bequeathed his art collection to the city. Roos House, built in 1813, displays about forty paintings from the golden age of Finnish art, around 1880–1910. Right next door, the Pedagogio school, completed in 1696, is Finland’s oldest wooden urban building other than a church. The museum opens Tuesday through Sunday at 11 a.m.

The British asked for it back; Kokkola kept it: an armed British naval launch is displayed in English Park (Englanninpuisto). During the Crimean War, Finland was part of the Russian Empire, which was at war with the United Kingdom. On June 7, 1854, nine British launches attacked the harbor. Soldiers and volunteers repelled them and captured this one, which still bears signs of the fighting. You can view it behind glass in its shelter in the park: allow twenty minutes.

activities.text: Look for porcelain dogs in the windows of Neristan, Kokkola’s old town. Their position indicated whether the sailor of the household was home or at sea. Some windows also have mirrors mounted outside, allowing residents to watch the street without going out. Neristan means “lower town” in Swedish. Sailors, craftspeople, and fishermen lived here, in twelve blocks of wooden houses built mainly in the 19th century. Ask Visit Kokkola for the free walking tour map, also available on your phone.

visits.text: The summit of Ukko-Koli at 347 meters is the highest point in southern Finland—and the view from the white quartzite cliff over Lake Pielinen is considered the country's most iconic national landscape. Jean Sibelius came here in 1904 and composed part of his Third Symphony. Painter Eero Järnefelt captured these hills on a canvas so famous it still adorns the restaurant in Helsinki's central station. The rock itself is among the oldest in continental Europe—remnants of a mountain range equivalent to the Himalayas formed 1.8 billion years ago. The climb from the Ukko Nature Centre takes 10 minutes on foot (800 m).

The Peaks Trail (1.3 km from Ukko-Koli) links the three main peaks named after gods from Finnish mythology: Ukko the God of the Sky (347 m), Akka the Female Spirit (338 m) and Paha the Evil Spirit (334 m). The site was considered sacred until the 18th century and was not inhabited until 200 years after the surrounding areas - people were afraid to live there. Pirunkirkko Cave (Devil's Church), 34 metres long, lies approximately 12 km from Koli, an 18-minute drive away: look for it, as it is well hidden.

The Räsävaara observation tower offers a radically different angle from Ukko-Koli—from the eastern side of the park, you get views over interior forests and lakes, not Pielinen. A less-visited detour showing the wildest face of Karelian forests.

activities.text: For a full day at Koli, take the Mäkränaho loop (7 km) from the summits—it descends into old-growth forests where Eero Järnefelt came to paint his autumn landscapes. You'll pass through slash-and-burn meadows (remnants of vanished farming practices), birch and pine forests, and rocky outcrops with beautiful views. The terrain is varied and sometimes slippery on the rocks—bring sturdy shoes.

A cruise on Lake Pielinen from Koli harbor lets you see the cliffs from the water—the same perspective that inspired Sibelius and the painters of Finland's national romantic era, but from the lake. Pielinen is Finland's fourth-largest lake: 93 km long, the horizons are vast. Summer boat excursions depart from Koli harbor.

The Herajärvi trail (20+ km) is Koli's challenge for experienced hikers—forests, bogs, wild lakes, and shelters with firewood for camping. If you're looking to spend a night deep in Karelian wilderness, this is your option. Plan for two days and inform someone of your route.

visits.text: Loviisa was founded in 1745 as a fortified border town against Russia and renamed in 1752 by King Adolf Frederick in honor of his wife, Queen Lovisa Ulrika—hence its nickname “the queen's town”. Its historic center miraculously survived the great fire of 1855 and remains one of Finland's best-preserved groups of wooden houses. The market at Laivasilta harbor offers lovely sea views and access to restaurants with terraces. Plan a round trip from Kotka within the day.

Malmgård Manor has belonged to the Creutz family for over 400 years—its current owner is the 14th representative. The present main building, in exposed brick with Neo-Renaissance influences from northern France and the Netherlands, dates from the 19th century. Above all, this is a working organic farm: cereals, a craft brewery, and award-winning flours. The farm shop is worth a stop. Plan a round trip from Kotka within the day.

Strömfors Ironworks, in Ruotsinpyhtää, was founded in 1698—the village's Swedish name comes directly from its 18th-century owners: Anders Nohrström and Jacob Forsell. The red and white wooden buildings characteristic of the Nordic countries still line the Kymi River. Now converted into an open-air museum, they house craft workshops, galleries, restaurants, and a water-powered hammer—the only one still operating in the country. If you visit in the right season, look out for forging demonstrations. Allow approximately 30 minutes' drive from Kotka.

Valkmusa National Park is a vast coastal peatland between Loviisa and Kotka, crossed by wooden boardwalks. From Kotka, drive to the park's parking lot, then continue on foot along the boardwalks. An observation tower provides views across the moorland as far as the eye can see—a landscape typical of southern Finland, very quiet and little visited.

Sapokka Water Garden occupies a former natural bay transformed into a park in the heart of Kotka. Waterfalls, ponds, docks, and a wide variety of plant species make it one of Finland's most award-winning urban parks. Entry is free—it's an ideal stop at the beginning or end of the day.

The Maritime Centre Vellamo occupies a spectacular wave-shaped building on Kotka's old docks—metal and printed glass facades. It houses three museums: the Finnish Maritime Museum, the Coast Guard Museum, and the Kymenlaakso Regional Museum. The simulated ship's bridge lets you take the helm. Allow 1 hour 30 minutes to 2 hours depending on your interest in maritime history.

Five kilometers north of Kotka, the Langinkoski Imperial Fishing Lodge sits on the Kymijoki rapids, within a 28-hectare nature reserve. Tsar Alexander III fell in love with the spot in the late 19th century and had this wooden chalet built in 1889. Empress Maria Feodorovna did her own cooking in the kitchen—a photo of her on the kitchen terrace was found in St. Petersburg archives. The furniture is largely original, including the imperial couple's beds that mysteriously disappeared in the 1920s and were found at Kultaranta, the Finnish president's summer residence, before being returned in 1956.

Katariina Seaside Park stretches across promontories south of Kotka, with direct views of the Gulf of Finland. Outdoor sculptures, seaside paths, and picnic areas make it a pleasant walking space between visits.

activities.text: The Kymi River runs alongside Strömfors Ironworks and can be explored by canoe on calm waters depending on the season. Rental companies offer half-day outings amid forests and gentle rapids. Allow approximately 30 minutes' drive from Kotka to reach Strömfors Ironworks.

The islands off Kotka are former military bastions, some now accessible to the public. Varissaari can be explored by boat from the harbor—forest trails, fortification remains, and wrecks visible while freediving depending on the season. Summer crossings depart from Kotka harbor.
The Kiulu floating sauna lets you sweat on the water in Kotka's small roadstead, with a plunge into the Gulf of Finland to follow. Reservations are essential—time slots fill quickly in season.

visits.text: Hamina Fortress was built from 1722 under the Swedish general Axel von Löwen, following the model of Italian Renaissance bastioned fortresses. Six bastions—named after Finnish towns: Savonlinna, Turku, Helsinki, Lappeenranta, Hämeenlinna, and the central bastion—surround a radial town center with eight streets radiating from Town Hall Square. The Fortress Trail (4.5 km) circles the ramparts, passing through vaulted corridors and old casemates. Follow it clockwise from the Flag Tower. Hamina is approximately 52 km from Kouvola, about 40 minutes' drive.

Hamina's historic center can be explored from Town Hall Square, where the eight radial streets begin. Wooden houses from the 19th century and religious buildings (the Lutheran church by C. L. Engel, 1843; the Orthodox Church of Saints Peter and Paul) punctuate the walk. The central bastion, restored in the 1990s, hosts the Hamina Tattoo international military music festival in summer. Hamina is approximately 52 km from Kouvola, about 40 minutes' drive.

Verla Board Mill, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996, is approximately 32 km from Kouvola, about 30 minutes' drive. This industrial village from the late 19th century is one of the world's rare examples of a completely preserved small rural industrial operation—factory buildings, workers' homes, and period equipment. Right beside the museum, on a rock face above the rapids, you will find prehistoric rock paintings dating from around 7,000 BC.

Repovesi National Park regularly ranks among Finland's top 10 most visited national parks—and it is easy to understand why when you see the cliffs plunging into the lakes. Plan an excursion from Kouvola: drive to the park's entrance parking lot, then continue on foot. The terrain is rugged: pine and spruce forests, rocky hills carved by glaciers, and clear lakes. The classic loop from the main entrance connects several summits with breathtaking views, suspension bridges, and camping sites with firewood supplies. Bring sturdy hiking shoes—the rocks can be slippery.

Mustila Arboretum was founded in 1902. Plan a round-trip excursion from Kouvola. Across 120 hectares, it brings together nearly 100 species of conifers and 120 species of broadleaved trees introduced from around the world. It is especially famous for its Rhododendron Valley, spectacular in June when more than 50 species bloom simultaneously. Outside the flowering season, giant conifers—hemlock, grand fir, and Serbian spruce—create an unexpected atmosphere of primeval forest.

The Ankkapurha district, on the banks of the Kymi River, is Kouvola's former industrial heart. It has museums, historic buildings, and works by the architect Alvar Aalto—a foray into the region's industrial and architectural past. Plan a round-trip excursion from the center of Kouvola.

activities.text: Hamina's Fortress Trail can also be explored by bicycle—local rental companies offer bikes in season. From the ramparts, the view over the old bastions and their surrounding gardens is particularly beautiful in the evening. Hamina is approximately 52 km from Kouvola, about 40 minutes' drive.

Tykkimäki is Finland's third-largest amusement park—roller coasters, water attractions, and entertainment for children. If you're traveling with family or have kids with you, it's a solid afternoon option. Outside the summer season, check opening dates before visiting.

Lake Käyrälampi, recently developed, offers a sandy beach, an accessible dock, canoe, kayak and stand-up paddleboard rentals, plus a public sauna. A relaxing option at the end of your itinerary, just minutes from Kouvola.

visits.text: A slightly leaning, shingle-clad bell tower crowns Ulrika Eleonora Church in the heart of Kristinestad. Shingles are small wooden boards laid like roof tiles. This red wooden church was completed in 1700. Its predecessor was destroyed by lightning in 1697. Inside, look for the model ships: these are votive offerings, objects donated to the church as an expression of devotion. The church is used mainly in summer for services and weddings, so visit during that season, when it is most likely to be open.

If you visit just one interior in Kristinestad, choose the Lebell merchant’s house (Lebellska köpmansgården). Its furnished rooms show how a wealthy merchant family lived from the 1760s to the 1840s. The house dates from 1761 and became a museum in 1939. In 2026, it is open from June 1 to August 16, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays and from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on weekends; admission costs €5.

Kristinestad’s maritime museum (Sjöfartsmuseet) occupies the attic where ships’ sails were once sewn, on the market square. It tells the story of the town’s seafaring, boatbuilding, and shipowners—the people who owned the vessels. A second exhibition room at 62 Strandgatan displays models of the town and its shipyards in the 18th and 19th centuries. In summer, the main museum opens Tuesday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

activities.text: You will explore Kristinestad’s old town on foot. Founded in 1649, it was named after Queen Christina of Sweden. Nearly 300 wooden houses and outbuildings are protected here. Shipowners lived near the sea; the farther you get from the water, the smaller the houses become. Slip into Kattpiskargränd, which a sign describes as Finland’s narrowest two-way street. Near the church, two customs buildings dating from 1680 and 1720 recall the days when people paid a customs duty on entering town.

days_plan.itin_title: Ostrobothnia in 4 Days: Vaasa, Kvarken, and Wooden Towns

visits.text: A war interrupted construction of Kuopio Cathedral (Kuopion tuomiokirkko). Work began in 1805 but stopped in 1808 because of the Finnish War between Sweden and Russia. The church was not completed until late 1815, following neoclassical plans from Stockholm. Its altar faces west, so the main entrance faces the old Market Square and the harbor. The cathedral is open daily from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., and on Friday evenings from 6 p.m. to 10 p.m.

The 75 m Puijo Tower crowns the wooded hill overlooking Kuopio: at the top, you are 224 m above Lake Kallavesi. Opened in 1963, it was the first tower with a revolving restaurant in the Nordic countries. The restaurant floor makes a full rotation in about an hour. Walk back down through the forest: the hill has been protected since 1928, and three nature trails, each about 2 km long, wind through it. The tower is open daily; the elevator costs €8.90 per adult.

The Old Kuopio Museum (Kuopion korttelimuseo) occupies an entire city block: eleven wooden houses built between the late 18th and late 19th centuries. Their interiors show urban life through the 1930s: a pharmacy, a shoemaker’s workshop, and a wealthy family’s home. One parlor is dedicated to Minna Canth (1844–1897), Finland’s first major female writer, who championed equality. From mid-May through late August, the museum is open Tuesday through Sunday; during the rest of the year, only Friday through Sunday. Admission €8, free for visitors under 18.

It looks like a fortress, but Kuopio Museum was built in 1907 to house collections. Its architect, J. V. Strömberg, who also designed the market hall, drew inspiration from Finland’s medieval castles. It is the country’s third-oldest purpose-built museum building. Its three floors explore the history of North Savo (the Kuopio region), the natural history of eastern Finland since the time of mammoths, and beliefs associated with the seasons. Admission €15, free for visitors under 18; closed Mondays.

Most of what is displayed at RIISA, the Finnish Orthodox Church Museum, was rescued from war. During World War II, icons (holy images painted on wood), religious objects, and books were evacuated from parishes in Karelia and several monasteries. These territories were later ceded to the Soviet Union. Look for two 12th-century gilt enamel miniatures in Georgian and Byzantine styles. The museum is open Tuesday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and weekends from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m.; admission €12.

activities.text: “Mualiman napa,” the center of the world: that is the nickname Kuopio residents give their Market Square (Kauppatori). Finland’s tourist office describes it as the largest in the country. Along its edge, the market hall, a turreted Art Nouveau building opened in 1902, houses bakers, fishmongers, and cheesemongers. Try kalakukko, the city’s specialty: a rye loaf filled with muikku (a small lake fish) or perch and pork, baked for several hours. Cut off the top like a lid, then eat the bread with the filling.

End the day at Jätkänkämppä, “the lumberjacks’ cabin,” a 1950s forest shelter on the shore of Lake Kallavesi. Its smoke sauna is among the largest in the world: it has accommodated 108 bathers at once. This sauna has no chimney. It is heated for much of the day, then the smoke is vented out: the stones retain the heat for the entire session. Cool off in the lake between rounds. Public evenings take place on Tuesdays year-round, as well as Thursdays and some Fridays in summer: check the dates before visiting. The sauna is coed: bring a swimsuit, as rentals are not available on-site.

Board a boat at Kuopio’s passenger harbor for a one-and-a-half-hour cruise on Lake Kallavesi. This harbor is the busiest in the Finnish Lakeland. From the boat, look out at the shores and islands: in 2020, Kuopio had more summer cottages than any other municipality in Finland, around 10,500. Kuopio Roll Cruises’ “City & Islands” cruise operates from June through August, with fares starting at €19. It departs from the dock at the end of Kauppakatu, the street where Market Square is located.

If the weather is nice, finish at Väinölänniemi Beach. Locals call this peninsula surrounded by Lake Kallavesi “Vänäri.” The beach is 150 m long, and its sandy bottom slopes gently, allowing children to wade a long way out. Lifeguards are on duty from June 15 through August 31, and facilities include a dock, diving board, café, and beach volleyball courts. Changing rooms and showers are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. in summer. In winter, a hole cut in the ice welcomes the bravest swimmers.

visits.text: The best overview of the region is at the Karhuntassu Cultural Center in Kuusamo. Its Discover Kuusamo exhibition, running through December 2027, tells the story of the area since the last ice age through models, films, and games. You can also see part of the Pyhälahde hoard: 409 silver coins from the late 11th century, originating in Germany, England, Denmark, and the Arab world. The son of a small-scale farmer discovered it in 1896 while cutting hay. Admission is €15, Tuesday through Saturday.

In September 1944, German soldiers buried the bells of Kuusamo Church to keep them from falling into the hands of the Soviet army. German troops then burned the old wooden church, built in 1802, during the Lapland War, which pitted Finland against Germany in 1944 and 1945. The two bells were not found until 1959. They are now installed in the church rebuilt in 1951. Check with the parish to see whether the interior is open on the day of your visit.

If your last day falls on a weekday, set aside 1 hour for the Kuusamo Open-Air Museum (Kuusamon kotiseutumuseo). The museum occupies an old farm beside a lake. It depicts the daily lives and celebrations of farmers in this region bordering Russia. Until the 17th century, the region was inhabited by the Sámi, a seminomadic people of the Far North. Families from Savo and Kainuu, farther south, began settling here in 1673. The museum opens only in summer, Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

activities.text: You land at Kuusamo Airport, 6 km northeast of downtown. Finnair connects it to Helsinki daily, and other airlines add seasonal flights from Germany, Switzerland, or the United Kingdom. A rental car makes the trip easier, as the sights are spread out. The bus serving the trailheads generally runs only from late May to October. Then drive south toward Julma-Ölkky, a long, narrow lake enclosed by cliffs, about an hour’s drive away.

places.name: Lappeenranta

visits.text: Lappeenranta Fortress is the city's oldest quarter, founded in 1649 when Governor-General Per Brahe the Younger decided to establish a trading post on the peninsula jutting into Lake Saimaa. The Swedes began fortification work in 1722 under Axel von Löwen to secure the frontier after losing territory to Russia. In 1741, Russian troops seized it—the fortress remained Russian until Finnish independence in 1917. Most of the current buildings date from the Russian era. Today, within the ramparts are the Lappeenranta Art Museum, the South Karelia Museum, and the Cavalry Museum, as well as Finland's oldest Orthodox church, built in 1785. The cobbled lanes and old limestone buildings are worth a stroll.

Lappeenranta Harbor is the city's lively heart in summer—restaurant terraces, markets, concerts, and direct views of Lake Saimaa. This is also where the giant sand castle stands, rebuilt every summer since 2004 by international sculptors around an annual theme, using 3 million kilograms of sand. In summer, local pastries called Vety and Atomi—meat and hard-boiled egg turnovers sold since the 1960s—are available at the harbor market kiosks. Don't leave without trying one.

The Saimaa Canal Museum, accessible from downtown via the canal bike path, tells the story of the Saimaa Canal linking the lake to the Gulf of Finland. Construction began in 1845 and wrapped up in 1858—at the time, it was the largest construction project ever undertaken in Finland, costing 3 million silver rubles. Every lock is faced entirely with local granite.

The Imatrankoski rapids, which can be visited on a round trip from Lappeenranta, formed 5,000 years ago when the waters of Lake Saimaa broke through the Salpausselkä ridge. As early as 1772, Empress Catherine II of Russia came to admire them with her entourage—they are one of Finland's oldest tourist attractions. In the late 19th century, Imatrankoski was one of Europe's busiest destinations, with up to 14 trains a day from Saint Petersburg. In 1929, the hydroelectric dam dried out the riverbed. Today, from July to August (Wednesday to Sunday at 6 pm), the dam opens for 16 minutes: 400 m³ of water per second surge through the gorges to music by Sibelius played over loudspeakers. The show is free—stand on Koskisilta bridge or in Koskipuisto park for the best view.

The Valtionhotelli hotel, which can be visited on a round trip from Lappeenranta, was built in 1903 in Art Nouveau style as a castle beside the rapids. It is Imatra's most striking building. It replaced two wooden hotels that had burned down and was designed to welcome wealthy tourists from Saint Petersburg. Even if you are not staying there, the façade seen from the park is worth a photograph.

The Church of the Three Crosses in Imatra, which can be visited on a round trip from Lappeenranta, is a work by Alvar Aalto, completed in 1957—considered by specialists to be his most original religious creation. The main hall can be divided into three independent naves using sliding partitions, allowing parish use during the week. The three white crosses at the altar give the church its name.

activities.text: Lake Saimaa can be explored by kayak from Lappeenranta Harbor—rental operators offer half-day and full-day outings through the archipelago. It's the best way to grasp the scale of this 4,400 km² inland sea, with its 15,000 islands and 15,000 km of shoreline. The Saimaa ringed seal, with only about 480 individuals left in the world, lives exclusively in this lake.

A cruise from Lappeenranta Harbor into the archipelago lets you see Saimaa from the water—some cruises offer ringed seal watching in season (spring–summer). It's a rare experience: the Saimaa ringed seal is one of Europe's most endangered mammals.

Kruununpuisto park in Imatra, which can be visited on a round trip from Lappeenranta, runs alongside the rapids from Koskisilta bridge to the old rock engravings—royal signatures left in the rock by distinguished 19th-century visitors, including Emperor Pedro II of Brazil in 1876. A one-hour walk in a shaded, historic setting.

activities.text: The engine hums for 17 km as the boat follows the Lemmenjoki Valley through the pines to Ravadas Falls. There, a tributary drops about 10 m into the river. Established in 1956, Lemmenjoki National Park is Finland’s largest national park. It is also gold prospecting country. Prospector Niilo Ranttila found gold in Morgamoja Creek in September 1945. Machinery has been banned since 2020, but prospectors still dig with shovels. Lunch is cooked over a wood fire on the riverbank.

The Lemmenjoki Nature Trail is the best way to understand the valley in 2 hours. This loop of just over 4 km starts at the Njurkulahti parking lot. It follows an esker, a long ridge of sand and gravel deposited by water from ancient glaciers. Along the way, you pass old pits dug to trap wild reindeer. Across the river, you can see the homestead of Kaapin Jouni, the nickname of a prominent Sámi reindeer herder who died in 1956. His family lived there until 2004. The terrain is rocky but easy to walk.
