visits.text: The easiest way to get a sense of Levi, a ski resort in Lapland, is to ride the Gondola2000 gondola to the summit at 531 m. At the top, the Peak Trail (summit trail), a 600 m loop accessible to strollers and wheelchairs, circles the summit. Views extend to Pallas-Yllästunturi National Park and into Sweden. Every November, these slopes host a World Cup slalom: the winner of the women’s event receives a reindeer, which is cared for at a nearby farm. In 2026, summer lift operations resumed on June 6.

activities.text: The Päiviö Trail, nicknamed the Great Shaman’s Trail, explores Lapland’s culture through stories about shamans. In traditional beliefs, the shaman acted as an intermediary between people and spirits. Short but rocky in places, the trail leads to Taalovaara and Kellostapuli, two heights from which you can see the Ounasjoki River flowing below. Wear closed-toe shoes rather than sandals.

Set aside two to three hours to climb Kätkätunturi, a summit near Levi. Along the way, a wooden shelter open on one side, called a laavu in Finnish, offers hikers a place to rest. The Rykimäpolku, or Rutting Trail (the mating season), circles the massif over 13 km. Its signs recount animal courtship displays with humor. Set out in the late afternoon: in midsummer, Levi has 45 days without a sunset.

days_plan.itin_title: Western Lapland in 5 Days: Levi, Pallas, and Kilpisjärvi

visits.text: Artist Eva Ryynänen's workshop at Paateri, about 20 km from Lieksa, is one of eastern Finland's most singular places. Ryynänen (1915-2001) spent her entire life here carving wooden figures from Karelian mythology, and built with her own hands her house, workshop, a round gallery, and a small log church beside a lake. This isn't an institutional museum—it's the trace of an entire life lived in the forest.

activities.text: The Ruunaa rapids, 30 km from Lieksa, are Finland's wildest whitewater—the Lieksanjoki River flows 30 km with six successive rapids toward the Russian border. Local operators offer runs on traditional wooden rafts or kayaks with campfire lunch on the banks. The full descent takes about 4 hours and leaves your arms tired and your mind clear. Book ahead—this is the region's main activity and groups fill quickly.

If you prefer walking to paddling, the rapids circuit (about 30 km) follows the river, passes six rapids, crosses suspension bridges, and climbs to the Huuhkajanvaara observation tower with views over forests and bogs toward the Russian border. Marked in yellow, doable in a day.

visits.text: More than 200 bird species are spotted each year in Liminganlahti Bay (Liminka Bay), and about 160 nest there. The visitor center (Liminganlahden luontokeskus) explores their lives in the exhibition “The Eight Seasons of the Bird Year,” designed for all ages. The bay covers more than 12,000 ha. Since 2004, it has been on the Ramsar List, which identifies wetlands of international importance. Borrow binoculars for adults or children at the reception desk. In summer, the center opens as early as 8 a.m.

activities.text: Follow the 600 m gravel path, accessible to wheelchairs and strollers, to the Virkkula birdwatching tower. This two-level tower, with a covered lower level, overlooks coastal meadows: grasslands beside the sea where animals graze in summer. In spring, look for ruffs, shorebirds whose males display to attract females.

Sheep graze along the Rantaniitty trail, whose name means “shore meadow.” This 650 m gravel trail starts in the visitor center’s courtyard and is suitable for strollers. Grazing maintains the meadow. Without livestock or mowing, reeds take over, and the birds that nest in these grasslands lose their habitat. Near the center, the Kukkala garden showcases plants from the bay’s shores.

visits.text: A small paper mill town deep in the countryside, yet a Monet hangs on the wall: this is Serlachius Manor (Serlachius Kartano) in Mänttä. This manor house, built in 1935 and inspired by English country houses, was the home of Gösta Serlachius, paper mill owner and art collector. You will see paintings by Gallen-Kallela, Schjerfbeck, and other leading Finnish painters, as well as a haystack painted by Monet in 1891. The wooden pavilion added in 2014, designed by Barcelona architecture firm MX_SI, houses contemporary art. You can have lunch at the on-site Gösta restaurant.

Money from paper paid for the art collection, and Serlachius Headquarters (Serlachius Pääkonttori) tells the story of how. This classical building from 1934 was the headquarters of the G. A. Serlachius company. Founded in 1868 by Gustaf Adolf Serlachius, the Mänttä mill still produces toilet paper and paper towels, including the Serla brand. The exhibitions combine the history of the paper industry, life in the town, and works of art. The €16 ticket covers both Serlachius museums. In winter, they are closed on Mondays.

activities.text: Walk between the two Serlachius museums along the Love Trail, the “path of love,” which is about 2.5 km long. At the manor end, the sculpture park is a good spot for a picnic, and you can take a rowboat out on the nearby lake. The trail is not cleared of snow in winter and is unsuitable for people with limited mobility. In that case, drive: the two sites are about 3 km apart. Bicycles can also be borrowed in exchange for an ID.

If you visit between mid-June and late August, add the Mänttä Art Festival (Mäntän kuvataideviikot). Founded in 1993, it bills itself as the largest summer exhibition of Finnish contemporary art. The works fill Pekilo, a former factory at the foot of the paper mill’s smokestack. The exhibition opens daily from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. during the season. Outside the season, use that hour to stroll through the manor’s sculpture park.

places.name: Mariehamn

visits.text: The Pommern is Mariehamn's first big impression - a 96-metre four-masted barque built in 1903, the best-preserved cargo sailing ship in the world. Go aboard and explore freely: crew cabins, hold and deck. This ship rounded Cape Horn to carry grain between Australia and Europe - some voyages lasted four months. Next door, the Åland Maritime Museum traces three centuries of seafaring tradition over three floors with interactive exhibitions.

Stroll Torggatan, Mariehamn's main street, and push open the door of the Åland parliament - an autonomous region of Finland since 1922, demilitarised, Swedish-speaking, with its own parliament, stamps and flag. Mariehamn was founded in 1861 by Tsar Alexander II, who named it after his wife. Guided tours of the parliament are available in summer.

At the Åland Museum, don't miss the champagne bottles on display - in 2010, divers discovered a wreck in Åland waters containing 168 bottles of champagne dating from 1840. Some bottles were still sparkling when opened.

Kastelholm, 25 km northeast of Mariehamn, is Åland's only medieval castle. Built in the late 14th century to control the trade route between Stockholm and Turku, it hosted Swedish kings including Gustaf Vasa, was the scene of witchcraft trials in the 1660s, caught fire in 1745 and served as a quarry for local farmers in the 1930s. Restored between 1982 and 1989, it opens from May to mid-September with guided tours. In July, a medieval festival with jousting and craftspeople is held here - check dates if you're passing during that period.

The Jan Karlsgården open-air museum adjoins the castle - about twenty 19th-century farm buildings moved from different parts of the archipelago: windmills, barns, forge, sauna. If you're there on a Wednesday in July, craft demonstrations take place on site. Since the 1940s, the Midsummer pole has been raised here every summer solstice.

The Bomarsund ruins are a few kilometres from the castle, about 32 km from Mariehamn, 25 minutes by road - what remains of a gigantic Russian naval fortress built to house 2,000 soldiers, destroyed in 1854 by Franco-British forces during the Crimean War. Cut hexagonal granite blocks lie scattered across the site in a landscape of forest and fjord. Free access, practically always deserted.

The Eckerö Post and Customs House, at the western tip of the main island, about 35 km from Mariehamn, 30 minutes by road, is an imposing building - built in yellow Empire style in 1828 by C. L. Engel, the same architect who designed Senate Square in Helsinki. It was here that for centuries couriers and travellers embarked for the crossing to Sweden. In bad weather, this crossing of the Baltic Sea could be deadly - the Engel building is a reminder that even empires organise themselves around their most perilous routes.

activities.text: The Turku→Mariehamn ferry takes 5-6 hours. It's not a constraint - it's a crossing: the ferries are large ships with buffet, bars and panoramic decks from which the archipelago gradually reveals itself. Book a seat or cabin - in July the ferries are full on weekends.

Åland is a paradise by bike - flat terrain, quiet roads, free ferries between islands. Rental shops in Mariehamn offer day trips. If you only have one day, the Royal Postal Route west to Eckerö (about 65 km round trip) runs along the open sea and passes the old Post House built by Engel. Go in the morning: the low light on the sea is especially beautiful.

Degersand beach in Eckerö, 11 km from the ferry company's port, is one of the most beautiful sandy beaches in Finland - shallow water for dozens of metres, a landscape of pines and red rocks. From Mariehamn, allow about 30 km, 30 minutes by road. Avoid July weekends, when it can be crowded.

The return from Mariehamn is by ferry to Turku (5-6h by day) or to Helsinki (11h overnight with cabin). The overnight crossing is recommended if you're continuing east - you sleep at sea and arrive in Helsinki in the morning without losing a day's accommodation. Book several days in advance in high season.

visits.text: Mikkeli served as the Finnish military headquarters during the Winter War (1939–40) and the Continuation War (1941–44)—Marshal Mannerheim commanded operations from here. The Headquarters Museum, housed in the original building, recounts those years through maps, artifacts, and period documents. Nearby, the Muisti Center (War and Peace) and the Infantry Museum complete the group of museums. For anyone interested in Finnish military history, this is one of the country's most thoroughly documented sites.
Mikkeli Cathedral, completed in 1896, is considered one of Finland's purest neo-Gothic structures—64 meters of red brick dominating the entire city. The single-nave interior is simple and impressive.

The Astuvansalmi rock paintings, about 50 km southeast of Mikkeli, are the largest and best-preserved in Finland—over 60 depictions of moose, human figures, and geometric forms traced in red ochre 4,000 to 5,000 years ago on a rock face by the lake. The site is accessible on foot from a parking area and worth the detour if you have time.

activities.text: Neitvuori hill, which can be visited on a round trip by car from Mikkeli, offers the best panorama of Lake Saimaa and the forests of South Savo. The climb from the parking lot takes about 30 minutes on foot—from the summit, lakes and islands stretch as far as the eye can see.

The journey from Mikkeli to Helsinki (230 km, about 2.5 hours by train or 2 hours 45 minutes by car) can include a lunch stop at one of the region's manor houses—Tertti or Kyyhkylä offer buffets of traditional Finnish cuisine on lakeside farming estates.

Finnish Lakeland: Saimaa, Castles and Forests

visits.text: In 1944, retreating German troops burned down almost the entire village of Muonio, but its wooden church remained standing. Begun in 1817 and consecrated in 1822, it is one of the few buildings spared by the flames. It can accommodate about 600 worshippers. In summer, the church opens during the day on selected dates: check the hours with the parish before planning an interior visit.

The Muonio local history museum (kotiseutumuseo) occupies Emma and Alfred Niva’s homestead at Lahenrannantie 51. Its main house dates from the late 19th century and was moved from the hamlet of Kihlanki in 1982. Around it, a granary from the 1850s, a drying barn, and a boathouse illustrate rural life in the valley in years past. The museum opens only in summer: call the municipal cultural services office for opening hours.

visits.text: Nurmes is a small town on the northern shore of Lake Pielinen with a remarkably preserved wooden quarter called Puu-Nurmes—sloping streets shaded by birches and houses dating from the 1880s to 1930s. Wander for half an hour: this is one of Finland's quietest wooden ensembles, without the crowds of Rauma or Porvoo.

Bomba Karelian Village, on the shores of Pielinen, is a wooden reconstruction of traditional Karelian architecture—log houses decorated with ornamental carvings and paintings, an Orthodox chapel, spa, and restaurants serving authentic regional cuisine. This is the place to taste Karelian stew (karjalanpaisti), Karelian pasties, and local fish specialties in their original context—don't leave without dining here.

activities.text: The shores of Lake Pielinen around Nurmes make for beautiful evening walks. The lake stretches 93 km—from certain points on the shore, you can't see the other side, and you understand why Finns speak of their lakes as an inland sea.

visits.text: Head straight to the top floor of Oodi Central Library, nicknamed “Book Heaven.” You will find 100,000 items, reading corners, nine living trees, and a balcony facing Parliament. Oodi opened on December 5, 2018, the day before Independence Day. The national government and the city gave it to the Finnish people to mark 100 years of the country’s independence. On the middle floor, a workshop open to the public offers 3D printers and laser cutters. Admission is free, with weekend hours from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m.

days_plan.itin_title: Helsinki in 2 Days: Suomenlinna, Seurasaari, and Design

visits.text: Red wooden warehouses, a bronze statue, and waterfront stalls: welcome to Kauppatori, Oulu’s market square. The old warehouses now house bars, restaurants, and craft shops. The Toripolliisi statue, the “market policeman,” was unveiled in 1987. Standing 2.2 m tall, it honors the officers who once patrolled the square. Start here: the Rotuaari pedestrian street begins just behind the statue.

In 1901, the city brought its butchers under one roof, marking the birth of Kauppahalli, Oulu’s market hall. Architects Karl Lindahl and Walter Thomé designed it in the Gothic Revival style, drawing on the forms of medieval buildings. A major renovation, completed in 2020, restored its original appearance. Inside, you’ll find local products, crafts, and souvenirs. Come for breakfast and try the salmon soup recommended by the tourist office.

“Pitch Island”: that is what the name Pikisaari means. This neighborhood of wooden houses is connected to the market square by a pedestrian bridge. Pitch is a black paste made from wood tar that was used to waterproof boat hulls. A pitch factory opened here in the 17th century, followed by shipyards and a sawmill. Artists and craftspeople live here today. In summer, visit the Sailor’s Home Museum (Merimiehen kotimuseo), housed in Oulu’s oldest wooden building.

Rain or shine, Oulu’s best attraction is also its newest: Tiima, a museum and science center that opened on October 9, 2026. It brings together the Tietomaa Science Center, the Oulu Museum, and VISIO, a room where images and sounds surround you. In the Masiina exhibition, you walk through an 1860s steam-powered robot factory. The factory is fictional, staged to look like a real industrial site. Then head up to the observation deck at the top of a tannery’s former water tower, about 45 m tall. Tickets cost €22 for adults and €14 for children.

Oulu Cathedral is named after a queen of Sweden, Sophia Magdalena, wife of King Gustav III. It was built in 1777, when Finland was part of the Kingdom of Sweden. The great fire of 1822 destroyed its wooden sections. Architect Carl Ludvig Engel rebuilt it using the old stone walls. The bell tower was not added until 1845. Inside, look for the portrait of Swedish historian Johannes Messenius, painted in 1611: it is the church’s most remarkable work of art. The cathedral is less than a 1 km walk from the market square.

Follow the Rotuaari pedestrian street to the small Kauppurienaukio square. Five large sculpted stones rise from the paving. This work, No.1574 Stone, is by British artist Rana Begum. Its shapes evoke glaciers and sea ice. It was installed in 2026, the year Oulu was a European Capital of Culture. It is a permanent installation. It belongs to Climate Clock, a trail of artworks about the climate, with the other pieces installed around Oulu. Allow 30 minutes, including the pedestrian street.

The Tähtitorni café, on the islet of Linnansaari, sits atop a gunpowder magazine from Oulu Castle. The castle was built in 1590 on an island in the Oulujoki delta. On July 31, 1793, lightning caused another gunpowder store to explode, almost completely destroying the castle. Only ruins remain. In 1875, the school for sea captains built an observatory on the surviving gunpowder magazine, hence the name Tähtitorni, “the observatory.” The café has been here since 1912. Its basement houses a small exhibition about the castle.

activities.text: You’re right in the city, yet sea trout swim up the streams of Hupisaaret to spawn. This park stretches across several small islands at the mouth of the Oulujoki, linked by bridges and dotted with old pavilions. It became a public park after the 1850s. At the northern end of the park, a fish ladder described as Finland’s longest helps fish swim upstream. It consists of a series of small stepped pools that they pass through one by one. Take a stroll here between visits: admission is free.

If the sky is clear, end the day at Nallikari Beach, known for its sunsets over the sea. The nearby tower, called “Nallikari Lighthouse,” is actually an observation tower built in 1988, with free admission. Oulu is close enough to the Arctic Circle that around June 21, the sun dips only about 1° below the horizon. Nights stay light, and daylight lasts 22 hours.

visits.text: Since February 16, 2026, Pallastunturi Gate, at the foot of the Pallas peaks, has been open to hikers around the clock without staff on site. This information building replaces the former visitor center, demolished in 2023 because of indoor air quality problems. Three screens display trail conditions and weather alerts, including the risk of forest fires in summer. Stop in before setting out: the heated room also provides shelter if the weather turns.

activities.text: The Taivaskero loop is the most scenic introduction to Pallas-Yllästunturi National Park. This 9 km trail climbs approximately 340 m to the summit at 809 m, the highest point in the park. At the top, a sign recalls an episode from the Helsinki Olympics. At midnight on July 6, 1952, an Olympic flame was lit here using the sun’s rays, since at this latitude the sun does not set in early summer. Allow approximately 3 hours and wear sturdy shoes: the rocky descent is slippery in wet weather.

If you arrive late in the day, the Vatikuru nature trail is enough to stretch your legs. This easy loop of approximately 3 km starts at the Pallastunturi parking lot and takes 1 hour to walk. It passes the ruins and memorials of the former mountain lodge built in 1938. German troops destroyed it in October 1944 during the Lapland War, which pitted Finland against the retreating German army. In summer, watch for reindeer in the parking lot: they climb to the bare heights to escape insects.

visits.text: Naantali, about a forty-minute drive from Pargas, has a wooden old town sloping down toward a lively marina. Naantali Church, founded as part of a Bridgettine convent in 1443, is the country's second-largest medieval church. From the harbour, look for the flag on the island of Luonnonmaa: when it is flying over Kultaranta villa, the President of the Republic is in summer residence.

About a forty-minute drive from Pargas, Moominworld stands on the island of Kailo, linked to central Naantali by a pedestrian bridge. Tove Jansson received the park's first key on its opening day in 1993. The experience is narrative: you enter the setting of the books, not an amusement park with rides. It is ideal with children, but Jansson fans of all ages will find something to enjoy. It opens only in summer, so book online.

Pargas is your first leap into the archipelago. The 14th-century gray stone medieval church is typical of Finnish-Swedish coastal towns. Ten minutes' walk away, the Pargas limestone quarry—150 meters deep across 70 hectares, in operation since the 12th century—is visible from a free, completely unknown viewpoint.

activities.text: The Archipelago Route between Pargas and Nagu is driven by car with free ferry crossings every 15-20 minutes. No tickets, no reservations—you wait, you board. Plan the whole day to wander. Nagu, the marina self-mockingly dubbed the “Riviera of the Finnish archipelago”, is tonight's stop.

visits.text: Everything in Petäjävesi Old Church is made of pine: log walls, pews, galleries, and hand-carved chandeliers. Farmers built it between 1763 and 1765 under the direction of Jaakko Leppänen. His grandson added the bell tower in 1821. Look at the pulpit, supported by a statue of Saint Christopher with rosy cheeks. Added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1994, the church is open daily from June 1 through August 31, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Admission includes a 20-minute guided tour.

activities.text: Before leaving Petäjävesi, take a break at Heinähattu, a few steps from the old church. This shop and café, which also sells secondhand goods, is known for its homemade cinnamon rolls. It is open Tuesday through Saturday: stop by on a weekday before driving to Säynätsalo.

visits.text: Old Porvoo is one of Finland's best-preserved medieval towns—the country's second-oldest city, founded in the 14th century, with town rights granted in 1346. Its cobblestone lanes and colorful wooden houses date mainly from the 18th and 19th centuries. The iconic image is the red ochre warehouses lining the Porvoonjoki River—built in the 1760s to store spices, wines, and tobacco imported by boat. The red color was reportedly first applied to welcome King Gustav III with dignity. Cross the Old Bridge for the best overall view: cathedral on the hill, warehouses in the water, colorful facades—this is the Porvoo photo.

Porvoo Cathedral crowns the old town from a hilltop. Built mainly in the 15th century from granite, it has endured fires, bombardments, and even a burglary throughout its 700-year history. This is where, in 1809, during the Diet of Porvoo, Tsar Alexander I granted Finland its autonomy as a Grand Duchy of Russia—a pivotal moment in Finnish history. A commemorative plaque inside recalls this event.

The home of J.L. Runeberg, Finland's national poet, is the country's oldest house museum—opened to the public as early as 1882. Runeberg settled here in 1852 to teach Greek literature and spent his last 25 years in this house, 14 of them bedridden following a stroke. Everything is original: wallpapers, library, hunting weapons in the 'fox fur room.' His wife Fredrika also invented the almond and arrack tart that bears his name—available year-round in Porvoo, though elsewhere in Finland it's only sold in January-February.

Albert Edelfelt's studio lies a few kilometers from the center, in Haikko. Edelfelt, born in Porvoo in 1854, spent 26 summers in the area and painted over 220 works there—some won prizes in Paris and were acquired by international museum collections. The studio built in 1883 now functions as a museum: you can see his belongings, sketches, and letters to his mother, in which he wrote that he feared above all “becoming a failure”. He died in Haikko in 1905, at age 51.

Holm House, built in 1763, immerses you in the home of a wealthy 18th-century merchant. The Gustavian furniture, china, and silverware are all from the period. It adjoins the Porvoo Museum, housed in the former town hall from 1764 on Raatihuoneentori Square—one of Finland's oldest surviving town halls.

activities.text: In summer, a steamboat connects Helsinki to Porvoo, sailing up the coast and the Porvoonjoki—the crossing takes about 3 hours 30 minutes and passes Haikko Manor. If you arrive by boat, return by bus (the reverse trip takes 1 hour 10 minutes) to make the most of your day. Check schedules in advance as departures are limited.

The Porvoo archipelago can be explored by boat from the harbor. Kråkö Island features gardens, artisan workshops, and coastal trails—the crossing is short and the atmosphere evokes the 19th-century Finnish archipelago, without crowds.

visits.text: A seaside castle that lost its sea: that is Raseborg Castle (Raseborgs slott), now in ruins. It was built in the 1370s on a rock surrounded by water to monitor trade in the Gulf of Finland. Since the last ice age, the land, freed from the weight of the ice, has been slowly rising. The sea therefore receded, making it increasingly difficult for boats to approach. This was one reason the castle was abandoned in the 16th century. Budget €8.50 and wear sturdy shoes: the stairs are steep.

activities.text: Walk to the Forngården Farm Museum along Lemmenpolku, the “Lovers’ Path,” a narrow forest trail about 500 m long. This open-air museum shows life on an archipelago farm in the mid-19th century. Parts of the main house date to the 18th century, and it is surrounded by a barn, storage sheds, and a smithy. On your way back, stop at Café Slottsknekten, which opened beside the ruins in 1893 to welcome tourists.

days_plan.itin_title: Finland’s Southern Coast in 3 Days: Fiskars, Ekenäs, and Hanko

visits.text: Why has the Kvarken Archipelago been UNESCO-listed since 2006? The Världsarvsporten visitor center, the “World Heritage Gateway,” explains why at the foot of the Replot Bridge. During the last ice age, a layer of ice about 3 km thick pushed the ground down. Since the ice melted, the land has been rising like a mattress returning to its original shape, at about 8 mm per year. The archipelago thus gains nearly one square kilometer of land each year: this phenomenon is the main reason for its listing. Admission to the Weichsel exhibition, named after this ice age, costs €6.

activities.text: You will cross the 1,045 m Replot Bridge to reach the island of Replot from the mainland. It is a cable-stayed bridge: its deck is supported by cables stretched from two 82.5 m pylons. It was inaugurated in 1997 by the Finnish president. After visiting the center, spend some time walking along the shore. The Vaasa tourist office recommends this short walk around the bridge.

places.name: Rovaniemi

visits.text: Arktikum is Rovaniemi's museum-science centre, recognisable by its 172-metre glass gallery extending toward the Ounasjoki River—an architecture that evokes a passage to the Arctic. Inside, two institutions: the Arctic Centre of the University of Lapland and the Regional Museum of Lapland. Exhibitions cover the Northern Lights (with scientific explanations and visual reconstructions), Sami history, life in the Far North, and the effects of climate change on the Arctic. Allow 2 hours.

Korundi, the House of Culture, occupies one of the few buildings in Rovaniemi to survive World War II—the former postal truck depot. Nearly the entire city was destroyed during the German retreat in 1944. Korundi now houses the Rovaniemi Art Museum (Finnish and Arctic contemporary art) and the Lapland Chamber Orchestra, the northernmost professional orchestra in the entire European Union.

Santa Claus Village sits 8 km north of the centre, positioned precisely on the Arctic Circle—or almost: the demarcation line in the village is actually 700 metres south of the true circle. The village welcomes over 700,000 visitors annually, year-round. In winter, you can cross the Arctic Circle, send a letter with the special stamp from Rovaniemi's official post office, and book husky safaris, reindeer sleigh rides, and snowmobile trips through village operators.

Ounasvaara Hill, east of the city, offers panoramic views of Rovaniemi and the confluence of the Kemijoki and Ounasjoki rivers. In winter, it is a family ski resort with illuminated slopes. In summer, hiking trails cross birch and spruce forest to the summit - allow one hour for the return walk.

The Jätkänkynttilä Bridge (Lumberjack's Candle Bridge) spans the Kemijoki in the city centre—it's illuminated at night and symbolises Rovaniemi's forestry history. It's the classic viewpoint over the river and the reflection of city lights.

Ranua Wildlife Park, 80 km south of Rovaniemi, is home to more than 50 Arctic species in natural enclosures: polar bears, lynx, wolverines, otters, wolves and wood bison. The walk through the park takes two to three hours, depending on your pace.

activities.text: Rovaniemi's urban plan was drawn by Alvar Aalto after the 1944 destruction—he designed the city in the shape of reindeer antlers when viewed from above. The main library on Hallituskatu, also designed by Aalto, is worth visiting for its indirect skylights and original Artek furniture. It's a working library—enter freely.

From late August to early April, the Northern Lights can be seen from Rovaniemi on clear nights. Local guides organise evening trips by snowmobile or on foot to open sites away from the city lights. Patience is essential - allow for several attempts. In summer, the midnight sun replaces the aurora: the sky does not grow dark between early June and early July.

A visit to a reindeer farm puts you in direct contact with Sami herders—you can feed the reindeer, learn about Arctic herding traditions, and in winter, take a short sleigh ride. Farms around Rovaniemi offer half-day and full-day visits. Book in advance during high season.

A husky safari in the forests of Lapland is a highly sought-after winter activity in Rovaniemi. Dog sleds set out early in the morning through quiet, snow-covered forests - conditions are best between December and March. In summer, walking trips with sled dogs are available. Booking several days ahead is essential.

The Ounasjoki River, flowing through Rovaniemi, can be explored by canoe or kayak departing from the city centre in summer—rental companies offer full-day trips to the forested meanders to the north. In winter, the same river becomes a snowmobile route across the ice.

A Lapland cuisine tasting in a downtown restaurant is a tangible way to close your Rovaniemi visit. Typical local menus include reindeer stew (poronkäristys) accompanied by mashed potatoes and lingonberry jam, smoked Kemijoki salmon, and Arctic berries (cloudberry, lingonberry) for dessert.

visits.text: Rukatunturi, a 492 m hill, is home to the Ruka ski resort on its slopes. From June to September, the Village-2-Valley scenic gondola leaves the village and crosses the hill in about 9 minutes to reach Ruka Valley, the new district on the eastern slope. Get off at the upper station, at the summit of Saarua, for views of the surrounding forests and lakes. You can then walk back down along the ski runs. Strong winds can stop the gondola: check that it is running before heading up.

Quiet in summer, the Rukatunturi ski jump comes alive in late fall. Opened in 1964, it is Finland’s largest ski jump. In late November, it regularly hosts the opening events of the World Cup season in ski jumping and Nordic combined (ski jumping followed by a cross-country ski race). The official record here is 150.5 m. If you visit at this time, book early: in 2024, the Ruka Nordic competition drew nearly 30,000 spectators.

activities.text: Start at the Saarua parking lot, on Ruka’s eastern slope, for the Valtavaaran huiputus trail: a 5.7 km loop taking about 1 hour 30 minutes. It climbs to the forest fire lookout hut at the summit of Valtavaara hill. Since summer 2026, Saarua has also been the southern endpoint of the Karhunkierros, the long-distance trail stretching about 80 km from the north. The reserve’s forests are home to the red-flanked bluetail, a small blue bird with orange flanks that has become the symbol of the area. Bring binoculars.

Evening light bathes Lake Konttaisenjärvi in gold at the foot of Konttainen hill. The Konttaisen kuhaus trail, a 2 km loop, climbs the hill in about 1 hour from the parking lot on Virkkulantie road. From the summit, the view stretches over Valtavaara, Ruka’s ski runs, and northern Kuusamo. Kuusamo lies about 60 km south of the Arctic Circle: from June 14 to 29, the sun barely dips below the horizon here. Head up late in the evening, when daylight lasts almost all night.

Pure fun, the Ruka Coaster is worth a ride between hikes. Opened in July 2025 on Ruka’s ski slopes, it is Finland’s first mountain coaster. An electric motor pulls the sled uphill, then gravity carries it down 767 m of track supported by pillars. You control the speed yourself with a brake handle, up to 40 km/h. Children can operate the sled from age 8, or ride with an adult from age 3.

visits.text: The best first look at the region is from the summit of Kaunispää, the hill overlooking Saariselkä. It is a tunturi: a rounded hill whose summit rises above the tree line, opening up the views. A road leads all the way to the top, at 438 m. From the 7.5 m observation tower, you can look out over Urho Kekkonen National Park. On clear days, the view reaches the hills beyond the Russian border. The panoramic restaurant at the summit offers a warm place to wait for the skies to clear.

activities.text: Stretch your legs on Aurorapolku, the “Aurora Trail,” which starts in the village of Saariselkä. The route is 2.1 km long with 35 m of elevation gain: allow 1 hour. It follows the Luttojoki stream, crosses it on a bridge, and passes through a small canyon. In summer, it is a good place to see the midnight sun: from late May through July, the sun never drops below the horizon. Bring mosquito repellent from mid-June to early August.

If the skies are clear between late August and April, watch for the northern lights between 9 p.m. and 1 a.m. These curtains of light, often green, ripple across the sky. They form in a ring around Earth’s magnetic pole. Northern Lapland lies directly beneath this ring. The Finnish Meteorological Institute records auroras here on about three out of every four clear nights. Head away from Saariselkä’s streetlights, for example toward the summit of Kaunispää.

visits.text: The Punkaharju ridge, which can be visited on a round trip from Savonlinna, is one of Finland's most famous national landscapes—a narrow strip of land formed 11,000 years ago by the retreating glacier, separating two lakes in the Saimaa system: Puruvesi and Pihlajavesi. The scenic road (7 km) follows the ridge between century-old pines, with water shimmering on both sides. Tsar Alexander I visited in 1802 and expressed his wish for it to be preserved—it has been protected since 1843, making it one of the world's oldest nature reserves. Drive slowly along the scenic road or cycle it—you will understand why this landscape has inspired generations of Finnish poets and painters.

The Lusto Finnish Forest Museum, located on the Punkaharju ridge, can be visited on a round trip from Savonlinna. It traces the relationship between the Finns and their forests over several centuries—a relationship that has shaped the country's national identity, economy and even architecture. The exhibitions are interactive and well designed.

Olavinlinna Castle—St. Olaf's in Swedish—is the northernmost medieval stone castle in Europe. Built in 1475 by Danish knight Erik Axelsson Tott to defend the Savo region against Russian attacks, it stands on a rocky islet in the middle of the lake, accessible by a narrow footbridge. Finnish soprano Aino Ackté discovered in 1907 that its walls offered exceptional acoustics and an exceptional setting for opera—the first festival took place in 1912. Today the Savonlinna Opera Festival draws 60,000 spectators a year, a quarter from abroad, in July. Outside festival season, the castle is open year-round with guided tours.

Kerimäki Church, 23 km from Savonlinna, is the largest wooden church in the world. Architect A.F. Grandstedt completed it in 1847: 45 meters long, 42 meters wide, 27 meters high, dome reaching 37 meters, 1,670 meters of benches seating over 3,000 people. An anecdote circulates: the architect supposedly worked in centimeters but the builder read the plans in inches—hence the outsized scale. The reality is more prosaic: the church was designed to accommodate half the region's population at once.

Riihisaari Museum, opposite Olavinlinna Castle, is the regional museum of Saimaa—it traces the history of the lake, the steamboats that plied its waters in the 19th century, and the Saimaa ringed seal. Historic boats are moored at the dock in front of the museum. The inner courtyard with its rocking chairs offers a peaceful view of the castle.

Savonlinna Cathedral and the harbor market form the city's beating heart in summer. The market sells muikku—vendace from Lake Puruvesi, whose local fishery holds a European Protected Geographical Indication. Try them fried on the spot: it's Savonlinna's signature dish.

activities.text: A cruise aboard a historic steamboat through the Savonlinna archipelago is one of the best ways to see Saimaa from the water. Some cruises offer themed outings: ringed seal watching, dinner on board, mushroom foraging in the fall. Inquire at Savonlinna Harbor.

Linnansaari National Park, accessible by boat from Rantasalmi (about 45 km from Savonlinna), is the heart of the Saimaa ringed seal's breeding area. More than 130 islands and hundreds of islets make up this park, which is explored from the water. Guided excursions depart from several access points.

Kolovesi National Park can be visited on a round trip from Savonlinna. This park of lakes and untouched islands is considered one of Finland's best kayaking spots. Kayak rental operators offer day trips or multi-day expeditions with camping on the islands.

visits.text: Säynätsalo Town Hall resembles a small hilltop town: red brick wings surround a raised courtyard overlooked by the council chamber. Aalto completed it in 1952, three years after winning the design competition. Climb to the courtyard using the grass staircase, with its grass-covered steps. In the council chamber, look up: Aalto nicknamed the fan-shaped beams supporting the roof “butterflies.” From June through August, the town hall is open daily, and admission (€11) includes the guided tour in English at 12:30 p.m.

To understand how Aalto worked, nothing beats the Muuratsalo Experimental House, 5 km from the town hall. Alvar and Elissa Aalto built it in 1952–1954 as a summer retreat on Lake Päijänne. The courtyard walls form around fifty panels of different bricks and tiles. Aalto wanted to see how each brick and mortar joint aged. Entry is only possible with a guide during the summer season, with tickets purchased in advance from Aalto2. The access trail through the forest is not suitable for wheelchairs.

visits.text: Senate Square (Senaatintori) is the best place to start getting to know Helsinki. Architect Carl Ludvig Engel designed the four major buildings surrounding it. The most prominent is the white Lutheran cathedral, completed in 1852 at the top of a broad flight of steps. In the center, the statue of Tsar Alexander II commemorates his reforms, which gave Finland greater autonomy when it was part of the Russian Empire. According to its 2026 opening hours, the cathedral is closed to visitors on Saturdays. Admission costs €8 from June to early November.

visits.text: “Finland in miniature”: that was the vision for Seurasaari Museum (Seurasaaren ulkomuseo), an open-air museum founded in 1909. On this wooded island, 89 wooden buildings have been relocated from across Finland: farmhouses, a parsonage, manor houses, and a windmill. The oldest date from the late 17th century. The museum is open from May 15 to September 15, from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tickets cost €14, and admission is free for visitors under 18. Through the end of August, the 3 p.m. guided tour in English is included in the ticket.

activities.text: You will cross Seurasaari’s white wooden bridge, where ducks, swans, and geese await walkers. The island is free to visit year-round, with a loop of about 3.1 km along sandy paths. Its red squirrels are used to visitors and often come close. To return downtown, bus 24 serves the island, and tram 4 stops at Paciuksenkatu, about 1 km away on foot.

visits.text: The Sibelius Monument (Sibelius-monumentti) brings together 569 welded steel pipes in Sibelius Park, by the sea. Created by sculptor Eila Hiltunen, it was unveiled in 1967 in tribute to composer Jean Sibelius. This abstract sculpture caused an uproar: some critics saw it as nothing more than an organ. To calm the debate, a portrait of the composer was added to a nearby granite wall. Step inside the structure: the pipes reverberate with echoes.

visits.text: Lake Kuusijärvi sits at the western entrance to Sipoonkorpi park—a natural starting point for the day. A sandy beach, two public saunas by the lake (including a traditional smoke sauna), picnic areas, and a pedestrian bridge leading straight into the park's forests. In winter, the bravest bathers practice ice swimming in a dedicated hole cut into the ice.

Sipoonkorpi National Park was established in 2011—one of Finland's newest and most visited, just 24 km from central Helsinki. Its very dense conifer forests, bogs, and rocky cliffs shaped by the last glaciation shelter the eagle owl, flying squirrel, and black woodpecker. The Byabäcken trail (1.4 km) is the shortest and most accessible—it runs alongside fields and a river with views of traditional pastures. If you have energy, the Kalkinpolttajanpolku (5 km) climbs to the summit of Högberget, the park's highest point, where views stretch to Helsinki's eastern suburbs.

In the village of Nikkilä, you'll find two examples of religious architecture from radically different eras side by side: the old medieval stone church from the 15th century and its 19th-century neo-Gothic neighbor. The contrast is striking from the road. Just behind, the former grounds of Nikkilä psychiatric hospital are now open for walks—the late 19th-century red brick buildings still stand in a strangely peaceful wooded setting.

Gumbostrand Konst & Form is an art gallery set in a former fishing village by the sea, east of Sipoo. Exhibitions rotate regularly and blend visual arts with quality crafts. If you're there in good weather, the waterfront terrace alone is worth the trip.

activities.text: The traditional sauna by Lake Kuusijärvi is open year-round. Plan an hour to enjoy the sauna and a dip in the lake—the water is cool from September onward. The experience is quintessentially Finnish and accessible without reservation.

The Sipoo archipelago can be explored by kayak or boat from Söderkulla: hundreds of islands and islets, barbecue areas on some, and an observation tower on Norrkullalandet. In summer, rental companies offer day trips—the water is calm and distances remain manageable.

visits.text: A plain of flat fields south of Vaasa is also a crater: Söderfjärden is the depression left by a meteorite impact hundreds of millions of years ago. It measures more than 5 km across. Land uplift raised it out of the sea, then pumps drained it for farming. The Meteoria center displays meteorites from around the world; in 2026, it was open daily from June 21 to August 9 (€10).

activities.text: If you visit in September, climb the Söderfjärden observation tower near the Munsmo pumping station. According to the city of Vaasa, this is where Finland’s largest gatherings of common cranes occur: more than 7,000 birds in the fall. In spring, from late March through May, the plain also attracts many migratory birds. Bring binoculars, as the plain is vast.

visits.text: Follow the Blue Route, marked with blue signs, from the main pier to the King’s Gate (Kuninkaanportti). This roughly 1.5 km path crosses Suomenlinna, a sea fortress whose construction began in 1748, when Finland was part of the Kingdom of Sweden. The site has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. The King’s Gate marks the spot where the ship carrying King Adolf Frederick of Sweden dropped anchor in 1752 during an inspection visit. Allow 1 hour to 1 hour 30 minutes of walking, excluding stops, and wear sturdy shoes for the cobblestones.

A church that also serves as a lighthouse: that is Suomenlinna Church. It was built in 1854 for the Orthodox soldiers of the Russian garrison. It became Lutheran when Finland took control of the fortress. Its tower still guides aircraft and boats: its light emits four flashes, corresponding to the letter H in Morse code, for Helsinki. The church is on the Blue Route, and admission is charged only from June through August.

If the weather takes a turn for the worse, the Suomenlinna Museum is a good place to shelter. Open year-round, it tells the story of the fortress, its restoration, and life there today: about 800 people still live on the islands. Several other museums, including the Vesikko submarine, are only open in summer. Each museum sells its own ticket, while the ramparts and squares are free to explore. The Museokortti, an annual pass valid at 360 Finnish museums, provides admission to most of Suomenlinna’s museums.

visits.text: From the top of the 20 m Saltkaret observation tower, the landscape of Svedjehamn resembles a washboard. These long, parallel ridges are De Geer moraines. They are ridges of stones and sand deposited underwater at the edge of the retreating glacier. Each is 2 to 5 m high and up to 1 km long. The tower is open year-round. A stroller-accessible path of about 1 km leads to it from the parking lot.

Red boathouses line the fishing harbor of Svedjehamn on the island of Björkö. The former fish-salting facility operated until 1989. Today it houses the Salteriet café and restaurant. You can also rent bikes there to ride along the small roads of the village of Björköby. Before leaving Vaasa, check the harbor webcam: it shows you the weather there.

activities.text: You will walk around Lake Bodvattnet on an easy trail of about 4 km, starting at Svedjehamn harbor. The path passes through Bodback, once Björkö’s main fishing harbor. As the land rose, the shoreline became too shallow for boats, and the harbor had to be moved. A few wooden boathouses and docks remain. In summer, Highland cattle, a long-haired Scottish breed, graze in the seaside meadows: keep your distance.

visits.text: Tampere residents call it “Vapriikki,” from the Swedish word fabrik, meaning “factory.” The Vapriikki Museum Centre does indeed occupy the red brick workshops of the former Tampella factory. A single €16 ticket gives you access to more than ten exhibitions: the Finnish Hockey Hall of Fame, the Finnish Museum of Games, natural history, or the mineral gallery. Choose three galleries rather than trying to see everything. The museum is closed on Mondays. Admission is free on Fridays from 3 p.m. to 6 p.m., except for a few exhibitions.

A serpent with leathery wings is painted at the very top of the vault in Tampere Cathedral (Tampereen tuomiokirkko). The church was completed in 1907 to designs by architect Lars Sonck. Its frescoes are the work of painter Hugo Simberg. The most famous, The Wounded Angel, shows two boys carrying an angel seated on a stretcher. Allow half an hour. The church opens daily from 11 a.m. to 3 p.m., and from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. from May 2 through August 31.

Tampere’s prettiest neighborhood? Probably Pispala, provided you enjoy climbing. Its colorful wooden houses cover Pispalanharju, Finland’s highest glacial ridge. This ridge is a long embankment of sand and gravel left behind by a melting glacier. Workers from Tampere’s factories once lived here. Climb the public stairways: from the top, you can see Lakes Näsijärvi and Pyhäjärvi. Near the summit stands Haulitorni, a tower built in 1908 where lead shot was manufactured until 1972. It is not open to visitors.

The restaurant in Näsinneula Tower completes a full rotation in 45 minutes, at a height of 124 m. Standing 168 m tall including its antenna, the tower overlooks Särkänniemi, Tampere’s amusement park, on a peninsula in Lake Näsijärvi. The elevator takes you up to an observation deck at 120 m, equipped with binoculars (tickets cost €7.90). Go up before nightfall to see the lakes. From April through October, the park’s rides also operate, including Konect, a family roller coaster that opened in 2026.

activities.text: If you try just one sauna in Tampere, choose Rajaportti in Pispala. Opened in 1906, it is Finland’s oldest public sauna still in operation. It is still heated with wood: a log fire heats a stove loaded with more than a tonne of stones. Once the fire is out, the stones remain scorching hot, and water thrown onto them produces steam. Men and women have separate changing rooms. Admission starts at €7.

visits.text: Helsinki’s most surprising church is barely noticeable from the street: Temppeliaukio Church (Temppeliaukion kirkko) is carved into rock. Architect brothers Timo and Tuomo Suomalainen completed it in 1969. Its walls are cut from granite about two billion years old. Left exposed, the rock gives the space acoustics prized for concerts. Above, a copper dome rests on a ring of windows that lights the nave. Admission is €8. On Sundays, the 10 a.m. service lasts about 1 hour 30 minutes, so come after noon.

visits.text: Nearly 50 buildings and structures spread across islands in the Oulujoki River make up the Turkansaari Open-Air Museum, about 16 km from downtown Oulu. The Ylikärppä farmyard shows rural life in the 1900s. The Parttuainen logging cabin tells the story of the men who cut timber after the war, then floated it downriver to sawmills. The museum opens only in summer: in 2026, from May 31 to August 30, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Admission is €12 and free for those under 18.

The most beautiful story at the Turkansaari museum begins with a simple cross drawn on a map from 1797. It marked a prayer house on the island, which was then deserted. Excavations uncovered its foundations in the early 1920s. The building itself, built in 1694 for fishermen, had been sold in 1814 and was being used as a warehouse in Oulu. It was brought back to the island in 1922, then consecrated as a church in 1925. Visit it first: the museum began with this church.

activities.text: Watch for smoke from the tar pit: every summer, the Turkansaari museum demonstrates how wood tar was made. Pine wood was burned slowly in a pit to extract the tar. It was used to waterproof wooden sailing ships. In the 19th century, Oulu was the world’s leading tar-exporting port. The Turkansaari café serves traditional Finnish snacks during opening hours.

visits.text: Start with Turku Castle - Finland's largest surviving medieval building, begun around 1280 at the mouth of the Aura River. Its heyday was 1556-1563, when Duke John of Finland installed a 600-person Renaissance court here with his Polish wife Catherine Jagiellon. She brought jewels, velvet, tapestries and forks - practically unknown in Finland at the time. Her older brother, King Erik, couldn't stand this display: he besieged the castle, imprisoned John and Catherine for three years, before a coup turned the tables. Allow at least 2 hours: the Renaissance halls, chapel and inner courtyards feel like a historical novel brought to life.

Turku Cathedral is the national sanctuary of Lutheran Finland - consecrated in 1300 on Unikankare Hill, it's the mother church of the entire Evangelical Lutheran Church of Finland. Its 101-metre tower was rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1827 that razed most of the city. Inside, look for the sarcophagus of Queen Karin Månsdotter, wife of King Erik XIV - imprisoned here after her husband's fall and died in Turku in 1612. It's Finland's only royal burial.

The Luostarinmäki quarter is an anomaly: the only part of Turku to survive the 1827 fire intact. About forty 18th-century wooden houses have been turned into a living museum where period-costumed craftspeople work in their original workshops - pottery, cutlery, shoemaking. The place is quiet and authentic, far from any tourist staging.

Naantali is 16 km from Turku - 35 to 50 minutes by bus from downtown. Its wooden old town slopes gently down to a marina bustling with café terraces. Naantali Church, founded on a 1443 Bridgettine convent, is the country's second-largest medieval church. From the harbour, watch for the flag on Luonnonmaa island: when it flies over Villa Kultaranta, the President of Finland is in summer residence.

Moominworld is on Kailo Island, connected to central Naantali by a pedestrian bridge. Tove Jansson received the first key to the park on its opening day in 1993 - she created the Moomins in 1945 during World War II as an antidote to anxiety. Here, no roller coasters: you step into the world of the books - the Moominhouse, Snufkin's camp in the forest, Snork's workshop. Perfect with children, but Jansson fans of all ages will find something. Book online - the park only opens in summer and slots fill up.

Rauma is about 92 km from Turku, 1 hour 10 by road. Old Rauma is the largest ensemble of wooden houses in the Nordic countries - 600 buildings over 29 hectares, listed by UNESCO in 1991. Don't expect a frozen museum: 800 people live here, surrounded by shops, cafés and craft workshops. The multicoloured neo-Renaissance façades date from the period of maritime prosperity at the end of the 19th century - in 1897, Rauma had the largest sailing fleet in Finland with 57 ships. Look for Kitukränn street: 2 metres wide, it is the narrowest in Finland.

The old Town Hall from 1776 on the market square, one of only two from that era preserved in Finland along with Porvoo's, houses the Rauma Museum with its collection on bobbin lacemaking - the tradition that gave Rauma its nickname 'lace town' since the 18th century. If you're there in late July, Lace Week (Pitsiviikko) transforms the old town into a festival with craft markets from across Europe and the spectacular Black Lace Night.

20 km from Rauma, the Sammallahdenmäki site is the town's second UNESCO site - 36 Bronze Age burial cairns dating from 1500 to 500 BC, scattered across a pine heath with marked trails. From Turku, plan a day trip, to combine with a visit to Rauma. It is quiet, free to access and almost always deserted.

activities.text: The Aura River runs through central Turku and its banks are lined with restaurant boats serving until midnight in summer. Walk from the cathedral to the castle along the riverside (3 km) and return by the opposite bank - you'll cover the whole city effortlessly. This is how Turku residents spend their summer evenings.

The Turku Art Museum, in an Art Nouveau building from 1904 on Puolalanmäki Hill, houses the most important Finnish art collection outside Helsinki. If you've seen works by Edelfelt or Schjerfbeck in reproduction, this is where you'll see them for real. Allow an hour to an hour and a half.

Set yourself up at the market on Old Rauma's central square - fruit, vegetables, smoked fish and local crafts in the morning. Café Sali on the square serves creative sandwiches and gives you a perfect view of the neighbourhood's comings and goings. It's the best place to grasp why Rauma is a 'living museum' rather than an empty showcase.

visits.text: Seven hundred thousand reclaimed bricks were used to build Uspenski Cathedral (Uspenskin katedraali). They came from Bomarsund, a fortress in the Åland Islands destroyed during the Crimean War, and were shipped across the sea on barges. Consecrated in 1868, the Orthodox church stands atop the hill in the Katajanokka district, east of the harbor. Inside, look at the iconostasis, the large icon-covered screen separating the altar from the congregation. Admission is €5; the cathedral is closed to visitors on Mondays. From September to April, it is open on Saturdays from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m.

visits.text: Visit the Ostrobothnian Museum (Pohjanmaan museo) before heading to the Kvarken Archipelago. Its Terranova exhibition explains land uplift and showcases coastal wildlife: seals, migratory birds, and the nest of a white-tailed eagle, a large sea eagle. A simulator shows the ridges of stones a glacier leaves behind as it melts. Another room traces Vaasa’s history up to the 1920s. The museum opens Wednesday through Sunday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; admission costs €15 and is free for visitors under 18.

Three painters created the altarpieces in Vaasa’s Holy Trinity Church. An altarpiece is the large painting placed behind the altar. Here, they are by Albert Edelfelt, R. W. Ekman, and Louis Sparre. Edelfelt belongs to the Golden Age of Finnish art, from around 1880 to 1910. The English Gothic church was inaugurated in 1869, in the city rebuilt after the fire of 1852. Visit outside service times: allow about 20 minutes.

The Kuntsi Museum of Modern Art occupies the former customs house on the waterfront at Vaasa’s Inner Harbor. Opened in 2007, it brings together two collections of modern and contemporary art. The first comes from the foundation established by Simo Kuntsi. The second was assembled by collector Lars Swanljung and donated to the city in 2018. It opens Wednesday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. The market square is just a few minutes away on foot.

Small in size, the Tikanoja Art Museum is worth a detour for its French paintings from the 19th and early 20th centuries. It occupies the house, completed in the early 1860s, where businessman Frithjof Tikanoja settled in 1918. The house became an art museum in 1951. Older Finnish art is also on display. The museum opens Wednesday through Saturday, from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.; it is closed Sunday through Tuesday.

In 1852, a fire devastated the wooden town of Vaasa: only 24 of its 379 private houses survived. The city was rebuilt 7 km to the northwest. In Old Vaasa (Vanha Vaasa), you will see the ruins of the stone-built St. Mary’s Church and the former court of appeal building dating from 1775, which became Korsholm Church. Look for the old stone quays, too: they now stand on dry land because the ground has risen. The Old Vaasa Museum is free and opens Wednesday through Saturday from May through August.

activities.text: You can pick up picnic supplies at Vaasa’s market hall (Kauppahalli), right in the city center. Its first hall opened on January 1, 1902, and the second in 1927. It houses seven businesses, including a fish shop and the Wasa Konditori tearoom. Shop here for the next day: in Svedjehamn, in the archipelago, a spot by the water is set up for picnics.

visits.text: The Finnish Aviation Museum sits 150 meters from Aviapolis station—you can't miss it. Opened in 1972 and moved to its current hangars in 1981, it houses over 80 aircraft tracing the country's civil and military aviation history, from early biplanes to Cold War fighters. The hangars aren't heated—bring a jacket even in summer, as the spaces are vast and metal holds the cold.

Heureka, Finland's science center, opened in 1989 in a building designed by architects Heikkinen and Komonen—mirrored glass facade facing the railway, white concrete interior. Its 3,500 m² of interactive exhibitions draw nearly 300,000 visitors annually, making it one of Finland's most popular leisure destinations. Don't miss the 135-seat planetarium or the Galilei outdoor science park, open in summer. You can easily spend 2 hours here with children.

The Fazer Experience visitor center in Vantaa tells the story of one of Finland's best-known chocolate brands. You'll journey through Finnish confectionery history from the late 19th century, with tastings included. The setting is modern and well designed for families—allow around 1 hour 15 minutes.

Tikkurilankoski and the banks of the Keravanjoki River offer a green escape in the heart of Vantaa. The park follows the rapids with walkways over the water—a pleasant way to decompress after the museums, far from any tourist crowds.

activities.text: The Myyrmäki district is home to the Lutheran church built in 1984 by Juha Leiviskä, whose luminous interior earned its architect the Alvar Aalto Prize. Around the church, the district's building facades display street art murals—an informal one-hour walk that makes a change from conventional sightseeing.
